Vulval dermatoses also more common postmenopause
Psychosocial impact | Hormonal changes affecting libido and body perception | Body image changes, pain, fatigue, psychological distress | Multifactorial; requires biopsychosocial and survivorship-focused care
Mental health and neurocognitive | Menopause <40 y doubles risk of depression (Georgakis et al. 2016). Early surgical menopause associated with increased dementia risk (HR: 1.89) (Rocca et al. 2007) | Chemotherapy-related cognitive impairment (up to 75%; persistent in ∼33%) (Rovito et al. 2025); psychological stress | Overlapping drivers; screen early and manage with supportive, behavioural, and pharmacological strategies
Bone health | Osteoporosis (8–14%) and osteopenia (23–57%) following surgical menopause, premature menopause, or early menopause (Gaba & Manchanda 2020) | Treatment-related bone loss; metastatic disease; AI. | High fracture risk; requires proactive screening (DEXA), prevention, and consideration of bone-protective therapies
Musculoskeletal symptoms | Increased sarcopenia (OR: 2.05) and musculoskeletal discomfort (OR: 2.26) with premature menopause (Vallejo et al. 2024) | Taxanes, platinum agents, PARPis, AI (treatment discontinuation up to 30%) (Nardin et al. 2025), anti-angiogenics. Higher risk of vitamin D deficiency (Zębalski et al. 2025) | Common cause of reduced quality of life and treatment non-adherence; requires symptom-directed management
Cardiometabolic health | POI increases cardiovascular risk (HR: 1.55) (Zhu et al. 2020) | Increased cardiovascular (HR: 1.37) and stroke risk (HR: 1.22) (Florido et al. 2022); cardiotoxic therapies and AI use | Additive risk; requires early cardiovascular risk assessment with long-term management and follow-up

In addition to menopausal symptoms, patients also experience cancer-related symptoms, treatment toxicities, and psychosocial stressors. These factors often intertwine with each other and can exacerbate menopausal symptom severity and negatively impact quality of life. Table 1 summarises the prevalence, severity, and clinical considerations of symptoms, highlighting the unique challenges faced by women experiencing cancer treatment-induced menopause. These symptoms rarely occur in isolation; cancer survivors frequently experience a convergence of symptoms that are driven by both menopausal hormonal changes and cancer treatment-related toxicities. Additionally, fatigue can act as a central amplifier of symptom burden, increasing the severity of hot flashes, mood disturbance, sexual dysfunction, and weight gain (Glaus et al. 2006). Understanding how these symptoms occur together and interact is important for individualised menopause management.

path: Menopause spectrum and impact of age at menopause on long-term health risks
sections.text:
Aside from symptom burden, a major concern is accelerated biological ageing and the associated long-term morbidity. Increasing evidence suggests that early loss of ovarian function contributes to biological age acceleration due to epigenetic changes, telomere shortening, and markers of cellular senescence (Zhou et al. 2025). In parallel, cancer survivors demonstrate treatment-related biological ageing, with similar alterations linked to increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk (Mandelblatt et al. 2021). Therefore, cancer treatment-induced menopause may be conceptualised as a ‘double-hit’ model. Both disruption of the endocrine system and cancer therapies increase biological ageing and long-term morbidity in this population.

A graded relationship is also observed for all-cause mortality across the menopause spectrum. A meta-analysis of seven studies showed that POI is associated with a 40% increased risk of all-cause mortality (RR: 1.40; 95 CI: 1.10–1.77), whilst EM confers a more modest risk (RR: 1.09; 95% CI: 1.00–1.18) (Tao et al. 2016). Similarly, there is a 55% higher cardiovascular risk in women with POI, compared with a 30% in those aged 40–44 years relative to the average age of menopause. This gradient is observed in a number of cardiovascular outcomes and persists even after adjustment for other risk factors (Zhu et al. 2019). These findings depict a dose–response relationship such that earlier loss of ovarian function is associated with progressively greater adverse health outcomes.

Bone health is also influenced by age at menopause, with earlier ovarian insufficiency associated with a greater risk of low bone density. Data from the Women’s Health Initiative Observational Study (n = 21,711) reported that menopause before 40 years was associated with a significantly higher fracture risk and lower bone mineral density (BMD) compared with menopause at age 50 years or older (HR: 1.21; 95% CI: 1.02–1.44) (Sullivan et al. 2015). Interventional data demonstrate that this risk is reversible, with hormone replacement therapy (HRT) restoring BMD in women with POI to levels comparable with age-matched controls over 12 months (Popat et al. 2014). In the context of cancer treatment-induced menopause, BMD loss is further increased. Population-based data indicate that there is a 10–30% excess fracture risk among cancer survivors compared with the general population (Ye et al. 2024).

Given this cumulative risk, early prevention strategies are essential. International guidelines recommend baseline BMD assessment at the time of POI diagnosis (Panay et al. 2024). If normal and appropriate hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is initiated, a repeat evaluation within 5 years is not required. However, if osteopenia or osteoporosis is reported, then repeat assessment is advised. Routine advice should include adequate dietary calcium, vitamin D supplementation, and weight-bearing exercise. Where HRT is not recommended, non-hormonal alternatives, such as bisphosphonates, provide comparable benefits in preserving BMD but are associated with different side effect profiles. Zoledronic acid not only improves BMD but also reduces the risk of breast cancer recurrence in postmenopausal women (Early Breast Cancer Trialist’s Collaborative Group 2015). Additionally, cardiovascular risk should be reviewed at diagnosis and monitored yearly, with optimisation of modifiable risk factors including smoking cessation, weight management, physical activity, blood pressure, and metabolic health (lipids and insulin resistance).

Early initiation of HRT in POI, if not contraindicated, can mitigate cardiovascular and bone risk and is advised by international guidelines (Panay et al. 2024, National Institute for Health & Care Excellence 2025), although long-term data are limited. Beyond the average age of menopause, decisions regarding continuation of HRT should be individualised, using the lowest effective dose with regular review.

path: Fertility, identity, and psychosexual impact of premature ovarian insufficiency
sections.text:
Infertility following a diagnosis of POI is one of the most distressing outcomes for women, particularly those who have not completed their family. Furthermore, the loss of reproductive choice along with the disruption of anticipated life trajectories contributes to the psychological burden. In a cross-sectional survey of 136 women with POI, including women with menopause as a result of cancer treatment, fertility was the most frequently reported specific concern (75%) (Singer et al. 2011).

The impact of cancer treatment-induced menopause also extends to broader aspects of identity and self-perception. In the same cohort, 78% of women reported that POI negatively affected their self-image and confidence. Menopause occurring earlier than expected may create a perceived mismatch between chronological age and bodily ageing, contributing to feelings of social isolation from peers who have not yet experienced menopause (Parton et al. 2017). Qualitative studies suggest that reproductive capacity remains closely linked to perceptions of femininity, thus contributing to the psychological impact of infertility and menopause (Parton et al. 2017).

Sexual dysfunction is also highly prevalent and multifactorial. It can include the loss of libido, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and diminished sexual confidence. These symptoms can negatively affect intimate relationships and are often compounded by fatigue, mood disturbance, and body image concerns associated with cancer treatment.

path: Gaps in menopause care for cancer survivors
sections.text:
Despite the significant symptom burden associated with cancer treatment-induced menopause, substantial gaps remain in counselling, access to specialist care, and symptom management among cancer survivors. Many women report receiving limited information beyond cancer risk reduction, with issues such as sexual health, cardiovascular risk, and body image often under-discussed. Consequently, survivors enter menopause with insufficient knowledge or support, amplifying distress and impairing quality of life. This is reflected in patient-reported survivorship data, in which menopause symptoms and associated health changes were reported to significantly impact quality of life in 86%, whilst 95% reported not receiving adequate support from their healthcare team during or after cancer treatment (Talaulikar et al. 2025).

Access to specialised menopause care is limited, with care commonly fragmented across specialities, primary care, and self-management (Peate et al. 2021). Effective therapies are often underutilised due to lack of resources, clinician uncertainty, concerns regarding oncological safety, and inconsistent guidance (Yongue et al. 2023). In the VIVROVAIRE study of ovarian cancer survivors, only 5 of 59 women (8.5%) received HRT despite 76% having no clear contraindication (Gernier et al. 2021). Additionally, patient-reported barriers, such as concerns about treatment efficacy, treatment cost, stigma, and inadequate clinician knowledge about treatment options (Hirschberg et al. 2025), further restrict timely intervention.

A key structural contributor to these gaps is the limited recognition of cancer treatment-induced menopause as a distinct clinical entity within existing healthcare frameworks. Menopause following cancer treatment is often subsumed within general menopause guidance, without adequately addressing the specific risks and survivorship needs of this population. This lack of tailored guidance has implications for service provision and care pathways. However, it is also important to recognise that whilst some patients require specialist multidisciplinary input, a substantial proportion can be effectively supported within current services, provided that clinicians are equipped with appropriate knowledge and resources.

Management of menopause following cancer treatment requires an individualised, risk-stratified approach that balances oncological safety with quality-of-life priorities and prevention of future morbidity. As symptoms are driven by both menopause and oncological processes, HRT alone often does not adequately address the full spectrum of symptom burden, and a multimodal management approach is required. Figure 1 provides a practical framework to guide clinical decision-making, integrating key considerations including oncological risk, symptom burden, and long-term health outcomes.

HRT remains the most effective treatment for menopausal symptoms and for the prevention of long-term sequelae of oestrogen deficiency in those with premature/early menopause. However, its use in cancer survivors requires careful consideration according to recurrence risk, tumour biology (see Fig. 2), and individual patient factors and preferences.

In women at low oncological risk, HRT can be prescribed and should be actively considered, particularly in those with POI. In this group, treatment is indicated not only to improve symptoms but also to mitigate the risks of long-term morbidity. HRT is recommended up until the average age of natural menopause (51 years) at which point its risks and benefits should be re-evaluated.

In women at intermediate risk, HRT may be considered following an individualised risk–benefit assessment. Non-hormonal treatments should be explored in the first instance; however, if they are not effective or there is patient preference, then HRT can be considered.

In women at high risk, systemic HRT is generally not recommended. In these patients, management should prioritise non-hormonal strategies and targeted local therapies where appropriate. For some women, an individualised multidisciplinary approach to HRT may be required if symptoms are severe and non-hormonal options are not acceptable or effective.

When prescribing HRT for women with cancer treatment-induced menopause, it is important to recognise that this population often carries a higher baseline risk profile. Oral oestradiol is an effective option and may be used in appropriately selected women. However, transdermal oestrogen is recommended in those receiving active cancer treatment or with comorbidities, such as an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (Vinogradova et al. 2019). Additionally, oral oestradiol should be used with caution in women at risk of drug interactions, such as those receiving systemic anticancer therapies, or in those with gastrointestinal malabsorption (e.g. radiation enteritis), as absorption may be unreliable.

Women with an intact uterus, including those who have undergone pelvic radiotherapy, should be prescribed an adequate dose of progesterone/progestogen for endometrial protection. This should also be considered in hysterectomised women with a history of endometrial cancer, or endometriosis where there is a theoretical risk of stimulating residual disease. The choice of progestogen may also be clinically relevant. Limited evidence suggests that micronized progesterone and dydrogesterone may have a more favourable breast safety profile in low-risk women (Fournier et al. 2007). Therefore, they may also be preferred in those with a history or increased risk of breast cancer, including BRCA mutation carriers. Off-label use of vaginal progesterone should be avoided in women who have undergone vaginal radiotherapy due to the risk of poor absorption.

path: Special considerations in hormone replacement therapy
sections.text: Tibolone is a selective tissue regulator with oestrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic activity and has demonstrated efficacy comparable to conventional HRT. Due to its weak oestrogenic activity, it is less effective at managing severe symptoms in POI. However, it does effectively improve BMD and reduce fracture risk (HR: 0.73; 95% CI: 0.59–0.92) (Barrionuevo et al. 2019). It may also offer a lower venous thromboembolism risk (RR: 0.92; 95% CI: 0.77–1.10 relative to non-use) compared with oral oestradiol (RR: 1.54; 95% CI: 1.44–1.65) (Renoux et al. 2010) and therefore provide an alternative option for poor transdermal absorbers. Although tibolone appears to have a less stimulatory effect on breast tissue and does not increase mammographic density, its oncological safety continues to be uncertain. The LIBERATE trial was terminated early due to increased risk of breast cancer recurrence in those with oestrogen receptor-positive tumours (HR: 1.56, 95% CI: 1.22–2.01, P = 0.0005) (Kenemans et al. 2009). Consequently, tibolone cannot be assumed to be a safer alternative and should not be prescribed where standard HRT is contraindicated.

path: Special considerations in hormone replacement therapy
sections.text:
Transdermal testosterone therapy at physiological doses for premenopausal women improves sexual function in hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) when other causes have been excluded and baseline serum levels are low. Current evidence does not support its use for cognition, mood, or musculoskeletal outcomes (e.g. BMD and muscle strength). However, trials such as the ESTEEM study are anticipated to address some of these evidence gaps (ISRCTN Registry 2025). Epidemiological studies have demonstrated that increased endogenous testosterone may be associated with increased breast cancer risk (HR: 1.18; 95% CI: 1.14–1.23) (Tin Tin et al. 2021). In contrast, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 250 women, with no history of breast cancer, reported that exogenous testosterone therapy did not significantly increase mammographic breast density, and short-term use was not associated with increased breast cancer incidence (Davis et al. 2009). However, the follow-up was only 52 weeks, which limits the ability of this study to establish the long-term breast safety of testosterone. A single-arm small pilot study of 29 breast cancer survivors undergoing ovarian suppression and aromatase inhibitor therapy evaluated a 3-month course of low-dose testosterone and demonstrated maintenance of baseline oestradiol levels alongside significant improvements in sexual function scores (Taranto et al. 2024). Long-term safety was not a reported outcome, and larger, longitudinal randomised controlled trials are required to assess this.

As there is limited information on the oncological safety of testosterone, particularly after hormone-positive cancers, such as breast cancer, and concerns over the peripheral conversion of testosterone to oestradiol, testosterone is not recommended.

path: Special considerations in hormone replacement therapy
sections.text: Tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors are associated with menopausal symptoms. Symptoms typically become apparent within 3–6 months of treatment, after which they often stabilise or improve (Marsden 2016). Switching endocrine therapies may help alleviate specific adverse effects (such as arthralgia and hair loss) but should only be considered in consultation with the oncology team.

path: Special considerations in hormone replacement therapy
Combined use of HRT with selective oestrogen receptor modulators
sections.text: The use of HRT with selective oestrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) is not routinely recommended. In selected cases if HRT is considered, switching from an aromatase inhibitor to tamoxifen may provide theoretical reassurance, as tamoxifen antagonises oestrogen receptors in breast tissue. Although bazedoxifene combinations show some favourable breast safety in the general population, they remain contraindicated after breast cancer.

path: Special considerations in hormone replacement therapy
sections.text:
Non-hormonal therapies play a key role in managing cancer treatment-induced menopause, especially in those for whom HRT is contraindicated or declined. However, their value extends beyond this subgroup of patients. As previously outlined, symptoms in cancer survivors often coalesce, due to the combined effects of endocrine changes, disease factors, and treatment-related toxicities. Therefore, HRT alone may not be sufficient to address the full range of symptoms or to improve quality of life. Also, confidence in counselling women on non-hormonal therapies facilitates patient choice.

Non-hormonal approaches can be used to target individual symptoms. These include pharmacological agents, behavioural and psychological interventions, and lifestyle-based strategies, each with variable efficacy. A tailored approach should prioritise the most burdensome symptoms, whilst accounting for comorbidities, concurrent cancer treatments, and patient preferences.

path: Special considerations in hormone replacement therapy
sections.text:
Pharmacological therapies (Table 2) can be less effective than HRT if used individually. Their use for managing menopause is off-label, except for clonidine and neurokinin receptor antagonists. Most prescribable agents target vasomotor symptoms, with individual selective benefits for mood (antidepressants), pain or arthralgia (gabapentinoids), and urinary symptoms (oxybutynin). As such, by providing targeted symptom control, they can achieve improvements in quality of life without complete menopause symptom resolution. However, for many women, the side effect profile of these agents outweighs the benefits of these agents, and longer-term complications, such as sexual dysfunction with the SSRIs and addiction potential (SSRIs/gabapentinoids), should be discussed before initiating treatment. Drug interactions must also be considered, particularly cytochrome P4502D6 inhibition in tamoxifen users.

Other pharmacological agents may offer selective symptom benefit. For example, mirtazapine can improve sleep and mood, although its use is limited by side effects, including weight gain, sedation, and cognitive effects. Daridorexant, approved for chronic insomnia where non-pharmacological measures have been insufficient, reduces nocturnal awakenings without significant daytime sedation. It should only be used as a short-term intervention with appropriate monitoring and coordination with primary care.

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is an evidence-based intervention grounded in a biopsychosocial model of menopause. Randomised controlled trials, including MENOS-2 (Ayers et al. 2012), have demonstrated significant and sustained reductions in vasomotor symptoms (50%) and improvements in sleep and quality of life with the use of either group or self-help CBT.

Lifestyle interventions provide modest but clinically meaningful benefits in both menopause symptoms and longer-term health. Practical measures, such as smoking cessation, reducing alcohol and caffeine intake, avoiding triggers and cooling strategies, alleviate vasomotor symptoms. Mind–body interventions (e.g. yoga, Pilates, and Tai Chi) may improve musculoskeletal symptoms, emotional well-being, and energy levels. Emerging evidence links diet and microbiome, with reduced intake of saturated fats and ultra-processed foods linked to improvements in cognition and mood (Cuozzo et al. 2026). Additionally, optimisation of modifiable risk factors can be beneficial for symptom management. For example, improving metabolic health can support cognitive function, whilst weight loss may improve both arthralgia and vasomotor symptoms (Anekwe et al. 2025).

Some may have oestrogenic effects or interact with cancer therapies and therefore careful counselling regarding safety and efficacy is required.

path: Management of genitourinary syndrome of menopause
sections.text:
Low-dose topical vaginal oestrogen is the most effective therapy for GSM with minimal systemic absorption. As such, it is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence as the first-line management of GSM (National Institute for Health & Care Excellence 2025). The main exception to this guidance is for those with breast cancer using an aromatase inhibitor (see also Fig. 2). For this subgroup, non-hormonal moisturisers and lubricants should be offered as a first-line treatment with escalation to vaginal oestrogen on an individualised basis. Furthermore, switching to tamoxifen may permit safer use but must be balanced against oncological efficacy (Baumgart et al. 2013). Where vaginal oestrogen is considered, the preparation choice may be relevant. Oestriol is a weaker oestrogen with a preferential affinity for urogenital rather than breast oestrogen receptors (Katzenellenbogen 1984) and does not convert to the more potent oestradiol in vivo. In women with persistent symptoms, consider irritant reactions or alternative diagnoses, such as vulval dermatoses, radiotherapy changes, or graft-versus-host disease, after allogenic stem cell transplants.

Alternative treatments for GSM include ospemifene and vaginal DHEA. Ospemifene is an oral SERM that improves vaginal dryness and dyspareunia by up to 80% at 12 months (Di Donato et al. 2019). It can be useful when vaginal treatment is impractical. However, there are no safety data for its use in hormone-sensitive cancers. Similarly, prasterone, a vaginal dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) insert, is approved for moderate-to-severe dyspareunia in menopause. In a randomised controlled trial of 464 women with prior breast or gynaecological cancer, it improved symptoms and sexual function without increasing serum oestradiol levels (Barton et al. 2018).

The management of menopause after cancer requires a multidisciplinary approach due to the complex and evolving needs of cancer survivors, which are shaped by disease characteristics, treatment exposures, comorbidities, and individual preferences. Despite this, access to specialist menopause services remains limited, and many clinicians report uncertainty on how to apply existing evidence to clinical practice (Yongue et al. 2023).

Multidisciplinary menopause and survivorship services offer a strategy to address these challenges, by offering expertise from oncology, gynaecology, endocrinology, primary care, and allied health. An example of this type of approach is the Menopausal Service after Cancer (MSAC) in Australia. This service is reported to have resulted in significant improvements in patient-reported outcomes, including vasomotor symptoms, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and sexual well-being (Hollingworth et al. 2022). However, such resource-intensive models may not be feasible in all healthcare settings.

A more practical approach is through the integration of menopause care within routine oncology pathways. Given the frequency of oncology follow-up, embedding menopause assessment and management into cancer care, supported by multidisciplinary discussions, supports the provision of individualised, evidence-based care whilst continuing access to specialist input (Brierley et al. 2026). Mind–body interventions, lifestyle modification, and non-pharmacological therapies can help improve overall well-being whilst complementing conventional treatments. Digital health initiatives have also been shown to improve symptoms, increase education, and empower patients with early menopause (Yeganeh et al. 2022).

A priority for future service development is the establishment of consensus across societies that recognise cancer treatment-induced menopause as a distinct clinical entity. There also needs to be clear guidance that delineates suitable care pathways. Existing models currently do not distinguish between patients who can be managed effectively in primary care and those requiring specialist or tertiary input. A stratified approach may help guide referral pathways and optimise resource utilisation to ensure that specialist services are targeted to those with the greatest need.

Despite increasing recognition of cancer treatment-induced menopause as a significant survivorship issue, there are significant evidence gaps. The international Menopause Priority Setting Partnership (MAPS) (Nash et al. 2024) and the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (National Institute for Health & Care Excellence 2025) have both identified key areas requiring further investigation. These include the identification of safe and effective non-hormonal therapies, particularly for women in whom HRT is contraindicated; optimisation of management strategies in breast cancer populations, where uncertainty regarding oncological safety persists; and clarification of the long-term safety, duration, and optimal regimens of hormone replacement therapy in higher-risk groups. In addition, high-quality longitudinal studies evaluating the safety of low-dose vaginal oestrogen in women using aromatase inhibitors and testosterone after breast cancer would also be of benefit.

Menopause induced by cancer treatment presents a unique and complex clinical challenge that extends beyond the natural physiological process of menopause. Its abrupt onset, combined with the effects of oncological therapies, results in a multidimensional burden encompassing physical, psychological, and social domains.

Although there is a growing awareness of cancer treatment-induced menopause as a significant survivorship issue, gaps remain in access to care, clinician education, and integration of menopause management within care pathways. Therefore, multidisciplinary and scalable models of care are required to address this unmet need. Such models would utilise specialist menopause services, integrate oncology pathways, and employ digital health interventions. Through a coordinated, patient-centred approach, survivorship and menopause care would balance both oncological safety and quality-of-life priorities.

Future research should focus on the safety and efficacy of therapeutic interventions in cancer populations, including hormone replacement therapy, novel non-hormonal agents, and integrative approaches. Additionally, greater emphasis is required on translating existing evidence into routine clinical practice.

Ultimately, improving outcomes for women with menopause induced by cancer treatment requires a shift away from the reactive management of symptoms and towards a more proactive integrative model that recognises menopause as an important component of cancer survivorship rather than a secondary consequence of treatment.

title: The Global Burden of Migraine: From Headache Days to Migraine-Affected Days—A Real-World Perspective on the Human and Societal Impact of Migraine

sections.text: Migraine research counts prevalence, migraine days, headache days, attack frequency, years lived with disability and disability-adjusted life years. People living with migraine experience something wider: pain, nausea, sensory intolerance, cognitive slowing, cancelled arrangements, lost working time, disrupted family life and the anticipation of the next attack. This review examines the distance between what is measured and what is lived and asks how many days of life migraine actually affects and how many can be recovered. We summarise the epidemiological foundation provided by the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021, then set out a conceptual framework in which total migraine burden is the sum of attack burden, recovery burden and functional burden. We describe the attack as a multi-phase event running from premonitory symptoms through headache and associated features into postdrome and functional recovery and review the interictal burden of anticipation, avoidance and unpredictability, which affects days on which no pain occurs. Occupational, economic, family and social consequences are considered alongside the treatment gap that keeps burden high despite therapeutic progress. Galcanezumab is used as an illustrative treatment example to examine how reductions in migraine frequency may relate to broader functional and patient-reported outcomes in clinical trials and routine practice. Interictal burden correlates only negligibly to weakly with monthly migraine headache days, which suggests that interictal burden represents a dimension that is not fully captured by migraine-headache-day frequency and highlights the importance of measuring, reporting and interpreting complementary patient-reported and functional outcomes alongside frequency. The proposed “migraine-affected days” construct is presented as a conceptual and hypothesis-generating framework, rather than as a validated clinical or psychometric measure, diagnostic criterion, or established treatment endpoint.

Migraine is among the most common neurological disorders and one of the leading causes of disability worldwide. In 2021, an estimated 1.2 billion people were living with migraine; headache disorders ranked as the second most prevalent condition globally and the third leading cause of years lived with disability (YLD), behind low back pain, major depressive disorder and age-related hearing loss [1]. These figures establish the scale of the problem. They describe how many people are affected and how much health loss is attributed to the condition at the population level.

What they describe less well is what a person with migraine actually experiences.

Migraine research counts prevalence, incidence, monthly migraine days (MMD), monthly headache days (MHD), attack frequency, attack duration, disability scores, YLD and disability-adjusted life years (DALY) [1]. A person with migraine experiences pain, nausea and vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia, cognitive slowing, an inability to work or drive, cancelled arrangements, disrupted family life, lost leisure time, fear of the next attack, unpredictability, a recovery period that continues after the pain resolves, and in many cases years of organising life around the disease.

The distance between these two lists is the subject of this review. Population-level estimates describe the magnitude of migraine. They do not fully describe what it means to live with migraine, and outcome measures inherited from population epidemiology do not automatically translate into the language patients use to judge whether treatment has worked.

The review proceeds in three movements. The first (Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Section 3.3, Section 3.4 and Section 3.5) establishes the epidemiological foundation and then widens the frame from headache days to affected days, tracing the attack across its phases, the interictal state, and the personal, family, occupational and economic consequences that follow. The second (Section 3.6, Section 3.7 and Section 3.8) examines why burden remains high despite therapeutic progress and what current outcome instruments do and do not capture. The third (Section 3.9 and Section 3.10) uses galcanezumab as an illustrative case to examine how reductions in migraine frequency may relate to functional, patient-reported and real-world outcomes. Galcanezumab is included as a worked example rather than as the subject of a comparative efficacy review.

Rationale for the study

The rationale for this review arises from a persistent discrepancy between how migraine is commonly measured and how the disease is experienced by patients.

Current clinical and epidemiological approaches provide robust and reproducible measures of disease frequency, particularly monthly migraine days and monthly headache days [2,3]. However, the burden of migraine extends beyond the days classified as migraine or headache days. An attack may involve premonitory symptoms before the onset of pain and postdromal impairment after the headache has resolved [3,4,5]. In addition, patients may experience anticipatory behaviour, avoidance of activities, uncertainty and functional restrictions during headache-free periods [6,7].

Consequently, the number of recorded migraine or headache days may not fully represent the number of days during which migraine affects an individual’s functioning and participation in everyday life.

This distinction is clinically relevant because the available evidence indicates that different dimensions of migraine burden are not interchangeable. Disability, quality of life, work productivity and interictal burden provide information that is not necessarily contained within a measure of headache frequency. In particular, the available evidence indicates only negligible-to-weak correlation between interictal burden and monthly migraine headache days, supporting the interpretation that these represent related but distinct dimensions of migraine burden.

These outcomes are often reported separately across different studies and are therefore difficult to interpret as components of a single patient-centred treatment benefit.

Elements of Novelty

The principal novelty of this review lies in its integrative approach to migraine burden. Rather than considering migraine frequency, disability, interictal burden, quality of life, productivity and treatment response as independent outcomes, the review examines how these domains are interconnected and how they collectively contribute to the real-world burden of migraine.

A further novel element is the proposal of “migraine-affected days” as a hypothesis-generating conceptual construct. The proposed framework extends the conventional counting of migraine or headache days by considering the broader period during which migraine may affect an individual’s functioning. It integrates three conceptually distinct components of burden: attack burden, reflecting pain and associated symptoms; recovery burden, reflecting premonitory and postdromal impairment; and functional burden, reflecting limitations and behavioural adaptations that may persist beyond periods of active headache.

A PubMed search conducted during preparation of this review did not identify prior use of the specific term “migraine-affected days” in the sense proposed here. The term is therefore introduced as a candidate construct for integrating dimensions of migraine burden that are currently considered across separate outcome domains. A candidate operationalisation is presented in Section 4.5 solely as a testable proposal and not as an established measurement definition.

The proposed construct is intended to provide a common interpretative framework through which existing evidence can be considered from the perspective of days of life affected and potentially recovered. It is not proposed as a replacement for established clinical endpoints and is not presented as a validated measurement instrument. Rather, it represents a conceptual and hypothesis-generating framework that may help guide future research toward outcomes that more closely reflect the patient’s experience of treatment benefit. The manuscript explicitly recognises that the proposed construct has not yet been operationalised or validated.

Finally, the review combines evidence from population epidemiology, clinical trials, patient-reported outcomes and prospective real-world cohorts. The use of galcanezumab as a worked example allows the relationship between reduction in migraine frequency and broader clinical and functional outcomes to be examined across different levels of evidence, without presenting galcanezumab as a comparative efficacy standard or implying superiority over other preventive treatments.

Aim of the study

The aim of this narrative review is to synthesise evidence on the multidimensional burden of migraine and to propose a conceptual framework of “migraine-affected days” that extends conventional migraine- and headache-day measures to include attack, recovery and functional burden.

Objectives

The objectives of this review are:To characterise the multidimensional burden of migraine by examining attack-related symptoms together with premonitory and postdromal impairment, interictal burden, disability, occupational and household productivity, and social and family consequences.To examine the limitations of conventional measures of migraine burden, particularly the use of monthly migraine days and monthly headache days as the principal indicators of treatment response, and to determine which clinically relevant dimensions of migraine remain insufficiently captured by these measures.To evaluate the relationship between reduction in migraine frequency and broader patient-relevant outcomes, including disability, quality of life, work productivity, acute medication use, interictal burden and transition between episodic and chronic migraine.To examine evidence from both controlled clinical trials and real-world studies in order to determine how the efficacy of preventive treatment translates into effectiveness and meaningful functional benefit in routine clinical practice.To develop an integrative conceptual framework for understanding migraine-affected days, linking attack burden, recovery burden and functional burden, while considering the potential distinction between days on which headache is present and days on which migraine meaningfully affects the patient’s life.To situate this framework against the endpoints currently recommended by the International Headache Society for controlled trials of preventive treatment, and to identify which domains are already covered and which are not.

This article is a structured narrative review addressing the multidimensional burden of migraine and the extent to which conventional frequency-based outcomes capture the broader clinical and functional consequences of the disease.

A narrative review design was selected because the objective was to integrate evidence from different methodological settings and across multiple dimensions of migraine burden, rather than to estimate a single pooled treatment effect. The evidence considered includes epidemiological studies, population-based and clinic-based observational studies, randomised controlled trials, secondary analyses of clinical trials, health-economic studies and prospective real-world cohorts.

The review was structured around the distinction between migraine frequency and the broader period during which migraine may affect patients’ functioning, behaviour and participation in everyday life. Accordingly, evidence was synthesised across attack-related burden, recovery-related burden, functional impairment, interictal burden, quality of life, productivity and treatment-related outcomes.

Given the substantial heterogeneity in study populations, study designs, outcome definitions, follow-up periods and healthcare settings, a qualitative structured narrative synthesis was performed. No formal quantitative meta-analysis or pooled effect estimate was undertaken.

The literature search was conducted using three electronic bibliographic databases:•PubMed/MEDLINE;•Embase; and•Scopus.

The electronic search was complemented by manual screening of the reference lists of relevant review articles and primary studies identified during the search process.

For the epidemiological component, evidence from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) programme was also considered. The review used the most recent published GBD analysis of headache disorders available to the authors to provide the population-level epidemiological context for migraine burden.

The selection of these information sources was intended to capture evidence from clinical, epidemiological, functional, patient-reported and health-economic research relevant to the objectives of the review.

Reference lists of relevant publications were subsequently screened manually to identify additional studies contributing to the predefined domains of the review.

For PubMed/MEDLINE, the search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and free-text terms addressing migraine and its multidimensional clinical, functional and societal burden. The Boolean operators AND and OR were used to combine the search concepts. The PubMed/MEDLINE search strategy was:

((“Migraine Disorders”[Mesh] OR migraine[tiab] OR “chronic migraine”[tiab]) AND (“Disease Burden”[Mesh] OR burden[tiab] OR disability[tiab] OR “Quality of Life”[Mesh] OR “quality of life”[tiab] OR interictal[tiab] OR premonitory[tiab] OR postdrom*[tiab] OR “work productivity”[tiab] OR productivity[tiab] OR absenteeism[tiab] OR presenteeism[tiab] OR “medication overuse”[tiab] OR “patient-reported outcome*”[tiab] OR “attack duration”[tiab] OR “migraine days”[tiab] OR “treatment persistence”[tiab] OR “real-world”[tiab] OR galcanezumab[tiab] OR CGRP[tiab]))**.

The search was conducted from database inception to 1 September 2026. No date restrictions were applied. No language restriction was imposed at the electronic search stage; however, only English-language reports were ultimately included in the narrative synthesis.

The last search was run on 1 September 2026. No language restriction was applied at the search stage, although only English-language reports were ultimately included. Searches were not date-limited, so that foundational instrument-validation and epidemiological sources published before 2000 remained eligible. As this was a structured narrative review rather than a systematic review, no duplicate-independent screening procedure or PRISMA-based quantitative accounting of records was undertaken. The implications of this approach are described in Section 2.6 and Section 2.11.

The review considered peer-reviewed epidemiological studies, population-based and clinic-based cohort studies, randomised controlled trials, prespecified secondary analyses and post hoc/exploratory analyses of clinical trials, health-economic analyses and prospective real-world cohorts.

Studies were considered relevant when they provided evidence concerning one or more of the following domains:•Migraine or headache frequency;•Attack characteristics and associated symptoms;•Premonitory or postdromal burden;•Disability and functional impairment;•Health-related quality of life;•Occupational and household functioning;•Absenteeism, presenteeism and work productivity;•Interictal burden;•Acute medication use and medication overuse;•Treatment persistence;•Transition between episodic and chronic migraine; or•Clinical effectiveness of preventive treatment in routine practice.

Case reports were excluded. Conference abstracts without subsequent full publication and non-peer-reviewed commentaries were generally excluded. Where an abstract represented the only available report of an otherwise identifiable dataset directly relevant to the review, this was retained and its limited publication status was taken into account when interpreting the evidence.

No restriction to a single study design was imposed because the review was intended to integrate evidence from complementary methodological approaches.

path: 2.6. Identification and Selection of Relevant Evidence
sections.text:
Potentially relevant publications were identified through the electronic database searches and manual examination of reference lists. Titles and abstracts were assessed for relevance to the predefined domains of migraine burden, followed by consideration of the full text of publications judged potentially relevant.

Study selection was performed by the review authors on the basis of relevance to the predefined scope and conceptual framework of the review. No formal duplicate-independent screening procedure was used. Where relevance or eligibility was uncertain, no formal adjudication algorithm was applied; such decisions were made on the basis of the predefined domains and the authors’ judgement regarding the contribution of the publication to the review framework.

Because this was a structured narrative review rather than a systematic review, no PRISMA flow diagram was constructed, and no formal quantitative accounting of records identified, screened, excluded or included was undertaken.

path: 2.7. Data Extraction and Organisation of Evidence
sections.text:
The extracted evidence was subsequently organised according to the three complementary domains defined in Section 2.2:

Attack burden: headache, associated symptoms, attack severity and duration.

Recovery burden: premonitory and postdromal symptoms and functional impairment extending beyond the period of active headache.

Functional burden: disability, limitations in daily activities, occupational and household impairment, productivity loss, social and family consequences, avoidance and interictal burden.

Treatment-related outcomes were extracted across these domains and included changes in migraine frequency, disability, acute medication use, treatment persistence, transition between episodic and chronic migraine, and real-world treatment effectiveness.

A structured qualitative narrative synthesis was performed.

Epidemiological studies were used to characterise the population-level magnitude and distribution of migraine. Clinical and observational studies were considered for evidence concerning attack burden, disability, functional impairment and interictal burden. Randomised controlled trials were used primarily to characterise treatment efficacy under controlled conditions, whereas prospective real-world studies were considered in relation to treatment effectiveness, persistence, tolerability and outcomes observed in routine clinical practice. These evidence streams were interpreted separately because observational studies do not provide the same basis for causal inference as randomised controlled trials.

path: 2.9. Interpretation of Different Types of Evidence
sections.text:
The evidence was interpreted according to study design and analytical status rather than treated as a single evidentiary body. For treatment-related conclusions, prespecified primary outcomes from randomised controlled trials were considered the principal evidence for efficacy. Prespecified secondary outcomes from randomised controlled trials were interpreted as complementary evidence addressing additional clinically relevant domains, including disability, quality of life and functional outcomes. Post hoc, exploratory or other analyses conducted outside the prespecified primary or secondary outcome structure were interpreted as hypothesis-generating and were not considered equivalent to prespecified trial outcomes. Prospective observational real-world studies were used to assess treatment effectiveness, persistence and outcomes observed in routine clinical practice but were interpreted separately from randomised evidence because their observational design does not provide the same basis for causal inference.

The analytical status of individual findings was based on the classification reported in the original publication. The review did not reclassify an analysis as prespecified, secondary or post hoc when this status was not clearly reported by the source.

This hierarchy represents an interpretative framework for the narrative synthesis rather than a formal GRADE assessment or quantitative ranking of the evidence. Accordingly, evidence from different designs was not assigned a numerical quality score.

Because this was a structured narrative review, no formal risk-of-bias instrument was applied across the included evidence. Consequently, the review does not provide a pooled estimate of the treatment effect or a formal quantitative assessment of certainty of evidence.

Galcanezumab was selected as an illustrative therapeutic example through which the relationship between reduction in migraine frequency and broader patient-relevant outcomes could be examined.

The selection was based on the availability of evidence across several clinically relevant populations and outcome domains, including episodic migraine, chronic migraine, patients with previous failure of multiple preventive treatment categories, functional outcomes, interictal burden and prospective real-world effectiveness.

Galcanezumab was therefore used as a worked example within the broader framework of migraine burden rather than as the subject of a comparative systematic review of preventive therapies. Its inclusion was intended to illustrate how reduction in migraine frequency may relate to changes in disability, function, interictal experience and other patient-relevant outcomes and does not imply superiority over other CGRP-targeted or conventional preventive treatments.

path: 2.11. Methodological Limitations of the Review Approach
sections.text:
This review was conducted as a structured narrative review rather than as a systematic review or meta-analysis. Accordingly, no review protocol was prospectively registered, study selection was not performed using duplicate-independent screening, no PRISMA flow diagram was constructed, and no formal quantitative accounting of records identified, screened, excluded or included was undertaken. A formal risk-of-bias instrument was also not applied across the heterogeneous body of evidence.

The selection of evidence therefore involved author judgement regarding the relevance of individual publications to the predefined domains and conceptual framework of the review. Although the search strategy included multiple bibliographic databases and manual screening of reference lists, the absence of duplicate-independent screening and quantitative accounting means that the possibility of selection bias or omission of potentially relevant literature cannot be excluded.

The heterogeneity of the evidence base represents an additional methodological consideration. The included studies differed in population characteristics, study design, outcome definitions, follow-up periods and healthcare settings, precluding a quantitative synthesis or direct comparison across all evidence domains.

The proposed concept of “migraine-affected days” should similarly be interpreted as a conceptual and hypothesis-generating framework emerging from the synthesis of existing evidence. It is not presented as a validated measurement instrument and requires future operationalisation and empirical validation before it can be considered for use as a formal clinical or research endpoint.

path: 3.1. Global and Epidemiological Burden of Migraine
sections.text:
The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 analysis provides the most recent population-level estimates considered in this review and demonstrates the substantial global burden associated with migraine and other headache disorders. In 2021, approximately 1.2 billion people were estimated to be living with migraine worldwide. Headache disorders collectively ranked as the second most prevalent condition globally and represented the third leading cause of years lived with disability (YLD), highlighting the substantial contribution of headache disorders to global non-fatal health loss [1].

The distribution of migraine-related burden was not uniform across age and sex groups. The highest burden was observed among women aged 30–44 years [1]. This concentration of burden in working-age adults is particularly relevant because migraine affects individuals during periods commonly characterised by substantial occupational, family and social responsibilities.

Temporal analyses from the GBD 2021 study showed that absolute numbers of cases and YLD increased between 1990 and 2021, whereas age-standardised rates remained broadly stable [1]. This pattern suggests that the increase in the absolute population burden was predominantly related to demographic changes, including population growth and ageing, rather than to a substantial increase in age-standardised individual risk [1].

The GBD 2021 analysis establishes migraine as a major contributor to global neurological morbidity and disability, with substantial variation across age, sex and healthcare-access settings [1]. Absolute burden increased over the period 1990–2021, whereas age-standardised rates remained comparatively stable, indicating an important contribution of demographic change to the increase in the number of affected individuals [1]. The principal quantitative estimates are summarised in Table 1.

Overall, the epidemiological evidence establishes migraine as a highly prevalent neurological disorder and a major contributor to population-level disability. However, these population-level measures primarily quantify prevalence and health loss and do not directly capture the distribution of individual days affected by migraine, the temporal extension of an attack beyond the headache phase, or the functional consequences occurring between attacks (Table 1).

path: 3.2. Migraine Days as a Conventional Measure of Disease Burden
sections.text:
Monthly migraine days (MMD) and monthly headache days (MHD) are widely used frequency-based measures for characterising migraine burden and evaluating the response to preventive treatment. Their use provides a reproducible and clinically interpretable estimate of the frequency of migraine or headache occurrence and allows changes in disease frequency to be compared across populations and treatment periods.

The burden experienced during an individual migraine day may also vary substantially according to attack duration and pain intensity. In a post hoc analysis of the phase 3 galcanezumab clinical development programme, total pain burden was assessed using a severity-weighted duration measure that incorporated the duration and maximum pain intensity of migraine headache. After accounting for migraine headache-day frequency and maximum pain severity, migraine duration on individual days accounted for the largest unique proportion of variability in total pain burden, representing 57.4% in episodic migraine and 61.1% in chronic migraine [2]. Thus, an identical number of migraine headache days may be associated with different overall pain burdens depending on the duration of individual attacks.

Taken together, the evidence demonstrates that MMD and MHD provide an important measure of migraine frequency but do not encompass the full temporal and functional burden of the disease. The available evidence identifies several additional dimensions including attack duration and intensity, premonitory and postdromal symptoms, interictal anxiety and avoidance that may vary independently from the number of recorded migraine days. Consequently, frequency-based measures should be interpreted as one component of migraine burden rather than as a comprehensive measure of the patient’s overall experience of the disease (Table 2).

The clinical burden of a migraine attack is not necessarily restricted to the period of active headache. The available evidence describes migraine as a temporally evolving process that may include symptoms before headache onset and a recovery phase after resolution of headache. These phases provide additional information regarding the duration and clinical impact of an individual migraine episode beyond the conventional count of migraine or headache days [3,4].

The premonitory phase may precede the onset of headache by hours and may include a range of non-pain symptoms. Reported manifestations include fatigue, changes in mood or activity, difficulty concentrating, neck stiffness, food cravings, repetitive yawning and increased sensitivity to light or sound [3,4]. These symptoms may occur before the onset of the headache phase and therefore are not necessarily represented by measures that define a migraine day according to the presence of headache. Quantitative studies consistently demonstrate that premonitory symptoms are common, while also showing substantial variation according to population, ascertainment method and symptom definition [9,10]. Across the available evidence, fatigue, neck symptoms, concentration difficulties and sensory symptoms are among the most frequently reported manifestations [4,9,10,11]. The quantitative estimates from these studies are summarised in Table 3.

The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3), recognises premonitory symptoms as part of the clinical evolution of migraine attacks and describes a postdromal phase following resolution of headache [3].

These estimates should not be interpreted as a single population-wide prevalence figure. Differences in study setting, participant selection, symptom definitions and methods of enquiry substantially influence the proportion of individuals reporting premonitory symptoms. In particular, clinic-based and event-based studies may identify higher frequencies than population-based studies [9,10].

The postdrome may last for up to 48 h and commonly includes fatigue, changes in mood and cognitive difficulties [3]. Thus, the temporal boundaries of a migraine episode may extend beyond the period during which the patient experiences the principal headache symptoms.

Prospective diary-based and observational evidence indicates that postdromal symptoms are common and may persist after headache resolution, with fatigue, cognitive difficulties, mood changes and neck symptoms among the most frequently described manifestations [5,12]. The available estimates vary substantially across study designs and populations, reflecting differences in definitions, ascertainment methods and risk of bias [12]. Key quantitative findings are summarised in Table 3.

Functional recovery did not occur immediately after headache resolution in all attacks. In the same prospective study, return to normal was achieved within 24 h after spontaneous resolution of headache in 93% of attacks [5]. Importantly, overall health-state scores remained lower during the postdrome than during the interictal period, indicating that symptom resolution and return to the patient’s usual level of functioning were not necessarily simultaneous [5].

The study also found no relationship between the medication taken for the acute headache and the duration of the postdrome, and migraine severity was not associated with postdrome duration [5]. These findings are relevant because they suggest that the persistence of postdromal symptoms cannot simply be attributed to differences in acute treatment or to the intensity of the preceding headache.

The premonitory and postdromal findings summarised above are set out in Table 3.

The burden of migraine may persist during periods without active headache. Interictal burden refers to health or well-being losses attributable to migraine that are experienced while the patient is free of headache and includes symptoms, anxiety, avoidance behaviour, functional limitations and cumulative consequences occurring between attacks [6].

The Eurolight findings are important population-based European evidence, but their estimates should not be interpreted as globally representative. More recent studies from non-European populations provide complementary evidence that interictal burden is also clinically relevant outside Europe, although differences in sampling and measurement instruments limit direct quantitative comparison across settings.

Evidence from large non-European populations provides complementary information. In the population-based OVERCOME (Japan) study, which included 17,071 respondents with migraine, 41.5% experienced moderate-to-severe interictal burden according to the MIBS-4. Among individual MIBS-4 domains, 26.8% of respondents reported that they worried about planning social or leisure activities at least some of the time between headache days, while 19.0% reported that headaches affected work or school at times when they did not have a headache [13]. A subsequent second-wave OVERCOME study conducted in Japan in 2023 included 19,590 adults with migraine and found that 47.1% had MIBS-4 scores ≥3, indicating moderate-to-severe interictal burden. Higher interictal burden was associated with greater disability, poorer migraine-specific quality of life and greater work and activity impairment, including among participants with lower ictal burden [14].

The broader literature therefore suggests that interictal burden is not restricted to the European setting. A systematic review published in 2026 identified 29 studies evaluating instruments or measurement properties relevant to migraine interictal burden. The MIBS-4 was used in 26 studies, compared with one study using the Eurolight questionnaire and two using the Fear of Attacks Inventory. The evidence base included large cohorts from Japan, the United States, the European Union and Spain, although the authors noted that evidence for several psychometric properties remains limited [15].

Taken together, these findings support interictal burden as a clinically relevant dimension of migraine, while also indicating that estimates obtained with different instruments and in different populations should not be assumed to be directly interchangeable.

Patient-reported assessment provides further evidence that interictal burden represents a dimension that is related to, but not synonymous with, migraine frequency. In a phase 3 preventive-treatment population of 462 participants, the Migraine Interictal Burden Scale (MIBS-4) was associated with migraine-specific quality of life, depressive symptoms and headache-related disability. In contrast, its correlation with monthly migraine headache days was low, with Spearman correlation coefficients of 0.21 at baseline and 0.32 at month 6 [7]. This pattern indicates that the number of migraine headache days alone does not fully account for the burden experienced between attacks.

The MIBS-4 evaluates several clinically relevant aspects of the interictal experience, including impairment in work or school, interference with family and social life, difficulties making plans or commitments, and emotional or cognitive consequences. Its use therefore provides a patient-centred approach to assessing consequences that may remain clinically relevant despite the absence of active headache.

The interictal findings discussed in this section are summarised in Table 4.

The burden of migraine extends beyond the occurrence of headache and includes measurable impairment in daily activities, occupational functioning, household responsibilities and social participation. Patient-reported outcome measures used in migraine research capture several of these dimensions, including disability, headache impact, health-related quality of life and productivity. Among the instruments most frequently used for this purpose are the Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS), the Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) and migraine-specific quality-of-life measures [16,17,18].

The MIDAS instrument quantifies disability according to the number of days during which migraine or headache interfered with work or school, household activities and leisure activities over a three-month recall period. The instrument therefore captures consequences of migraine in several functional roles rather than focusing exclusively on headache frequency [16]. HIT-6 provides a complementary assessment of headache impact, including effects on pain, daily activities, energy, emotional functioning and ability to concentrate [17]. Migraine-specific quality-of-life instruments further assess the effect of migraine on role functioning and emotional well-being [18].

Observational evidence demonstrates substantially greater functional impairment among patients with chronic migraine than among those with episodic migraine, across missed work or school, reduced productivity, disability, headache impact and general health-related quality of life [19]. The quantitative estimates are presented in Table 5.

The same study demonstrated an impact on broader health-related quality of life. Mean general health scores on the SF-36 were 39.9 ± 14.7 among participants with chronic migraine and 66.2 ± 18.2 among those with episodic migraine (p = 0.001) [19]. These findings illustrate that increasing migraine frequency is associated with a broader deterioration in functional status and perceived health, although frequency alone does not specify the mechanisms through which this impairment occurs.

The occupational consequences of migraine are also reflected at the population level. The economic consequences of migraine are also substantial, with indirect productivity losses representing an important component of the total societal burden [20]. The principal quantitative estimates are summarised in Table 5.

Evidence from the Eurolight project further demonstrated that lost productive time is associated with the broader interictal burden of headache. Participants with migraine reported consequences extending beyond the immediate period of headache, including reluctance to disclose their condition to others, difficulties with educational performance, reduced earnings and career consequences [6]. Thus, the functional burden of migraine includes both direct impairment during headache episodes and cumulative consequences that may develop across repeated attacks and the periods between them.

The relationship between headache frequency and lost productivity has also been examined using individual participant data from population-based studies. Analyses incorporating headache frequency, usual attack duration, headache intensity and productivity loss indicate that these clinical characteristics jointly contribute to the amount of paid and household work lost because of headache [21]. This supports the interpretation that frequency is an important determinant of productivity loss but does not operate independently of other characteristics of the headache experience.

The consequences also extend into family life, career trajectory and financial security. In the CaMEO study, among 13,064 respondents, 32.7% reported that headache had negatively affected at least one career area, rising from 30.3% in episodic migraine to 58.4% in chronic migraine, and 32.1% endorsed worry about long-term financial security because of migraine, rising from 29.7% to 57.4% across the same comparison. Among respondents in a cohabiting relationship, 3.2% reported that they had chosen not to have children, had delayed having children or had had fewer children because of migraine, rising from 2.6% in episodic migraine to 9.5% in chronic migraine [22]. These outcomes represent decisions not taken rather than activities interrupted, and no headache diary records them.

The economic consequences extend to unpaid as well as paid work. A German population-based analysis monetised productivity losses as gross value added and identified losses of tens of billions of euros annually in paid work, with a comparable magnitude in unpaid work such as household and caring activity [23]. Because unpaid work is disproportionately performed by the demographic group in which migraine burden peaks, its omission from cost models introduces a distributional error as well as an underestimate.

Stigma has recently been operationalised in this field and can therefore be treated as evidence rather than impression. The Migraine-Related Stigma questionnaire, developed in a population-based sample of 61,932 United States adults with migraine, resolves into two internally consistent subscales: an external perception of secondary gain and an external perception that others minimise the burden of the disease [24]. The second follows directly from a disease label that non-sufferers map onto their own experience of ordinary headache, and it plausibly contributes to the disclosure reluctance recorded in the Eurolight data.

Taken together, the reviewed evidence demonstrates that migraine affects several domains of functioning, including employment, productivity, household activities, education, social participation and perceived health. The magnitude of these consequences increases substantially with greater disease burden, particularly in chronic migraine, but the available evidence also indicates that functional impairment cannot be reduced to a simple count of headache days. Frequency, attack characteristics, interictal consequences and individual functional circumstances contribute to the overall impact experienced by patients (Table 5).

The quantitative estimates presented in Table 5 are intended to illustrate the range of functional and health-related consequences reported in the literature rather than to provide globally representative prevalence estimates. In particular, several of the clinical disability and productivity estimates derive from a tertiary headache-centre population and should therefore be interpreted in the context of the study setting and population characteristics.

path: 3.6. Treatment Gaps, Disease Progression and Medication Overuse
sections.text:
The population-level burden described in Section 3.1 persists despite the availability of effective preventive treatment. Two processes account for much of this: a large proportion of eligible patients never receive prevention, and a proportion of those who remain untreated progress to higher attack frequencies.

Consultation is the first filter. In the CaMEO study, among participants meeting criteria for chronic migraine with headache-related disability, 512 of 1254 (40.8%) reported currently consulting a healthcare professional for headache, and accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment act as successive further filters on the eligible population [25].

The scale of the preventive gap has been quantified across several countries. Population data have long indicated that a substantial minority of people with migraine meet criteria for preventive treatment while only a small fraction receive it [26]. The CaMEO-International study surveyed 90,613 people across six countries, of whom 14,492 met criteria for migraine and completed the full survey. Applying the American Headache Society 2021 consensus algorithm, 36.2% qualified for preventive treatment, and of those, 84.5% were not taking a preventive medication at the time of the survey [27].

A second gap is easily overlooked. Among respondents in that study who were currently taking a preventive medication, 50.2% still met the algorithm criteria for needing preventive treatment [27], indicating inadequate benefit from the regimen they were already receiving. The treatment gap is therefore a gap in effectiveness among the treated as well as a gap in prescribing.

The OVERCOME study reached a compatible conclusion in a United States sample of 59,001 participants, among whom 77.1% were candidates for initiation or modification of prescription treatment. Acute medication overuse was most frequent in the group with combined acute and preventive needs, at 37.0%, and moderate-to-severe interictal burden was reported by 69.9% of that group [28]. Severe interictal burden was most strongly associated with unmet acute treatment need, whereas acute medication overuse was most strongly associated with unmet preventive need [28].

Persistence on conventional oral preventives contributes to the gap. In a retrospective analysis of 8707 patients with chronic migraine, persistence with the initial oral preventive medication was 25% at six months and 14% at twelve months, and persistence declined further among patients who switched or re-initiated treatment [29]. A majority of patients therefore cycle through preventive medications without remaining on any of them.

Attack frequency is not static. Longitudinal population data indicate that a small proportion of people with episodic migraine transition to chronic migraine each year, with baseline headache frequency among the strongest predictors and with risk rising as baseline frequency increases [30]. Frequent acute medication use is both a rational response to frequent attacks and an established risk factor for progression [30]. Frequent acute medication use is both a rational response to frequent attacks and an established epidemiological risk factor for migraine progression, which may contribute to a cycle in which frequent reliance on acute medication is associated with an increased risk of migraine progression.

Reductions in acute medication days and cessation of medication overuse therefore act on progression risk as well as on symptom control, which is relevant to the interpretation of the real-world findings reported in Section 3.10.

The reviewed evidence indicates that the principal instruments used to assess migraine burden capture distinct and clinically relevant dimensions of the disease. Monthly migraine days (MMD) and monthly headache days (MHD) quantify the frequency of attacks, whereas disability, quality of life, productivity and interictal burden require complementary patient-reported or functional measures. The available instruments therefore provide partially overlapping but non-equivalent information about the patient’s experience of migraine.

The Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS) quantifies days of lost or substantially reduced productivity in work or school, household activities and social or leisure activities over a three-month recall period [16]. The Migraine-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire version 2.1 (MSQ v2.1) evaluates the effects of migraine on role-function restrictive, role-function preventive and emotional-function domains [18]. These instruments therefore extend assessment beyond headache frequency by addressing consequences of migraine for everyday functioning and quality of life.

The distinction between frequency and broader burden is particularly relevant when treatment response is defined primarily according to a reduction in MMD. A statistically significant reduction in migraine days demonstrates improvement in the frequency domain, but it does not by itself establish the extent to which disability, work productivity, acute medication reliance, interictal burden or social functioning have improved. These outcomes may change in parallel with migraine frequency, but they represent separate dimensions that require direct measurement.

Importantly, this should not be interpreted to mean that contemporary preventive-treatment trials assess migraine frequency in isolation. Current International Headache Society recommendations explicitly recognise responder rates, acute medication use, headache-related disability and health-related quality of life as complementary outcomes alongside the primary frequency endpoint [8,31]. The methodological gap identified here is therefore not the absence of multidimensional outcomes from contemporary trial guidance, but the extent to which these outcomes are consistently measured, reported, interpreted together and incorporated into an overall assessment of treatment benefit.

The available evidence provides empirical support for this distinction. As described above, interictal burden measured using the MIBS-4 showed only low correlations with monthly migraine headache days, with Spearman correlation coefficients of 0.21 at baseline and 0.32 at month 6 [7]. Thus, the number of migraine headache days cannot be considered a reliable surrogate for the burden experienced between attacks.

A similar limitation applies to response thresholds based exclusively on frequency. A patient achieving a predefined reduction in MMD may appropriately be classified as a treatment responder with respect to the frequency endpoint while continuing to experience substantial residual burden in other domains. For example, the patient may continue to experience severe individual attacks, require acute medication, experience anticipatory anxiety or retain functional limitations despite a clinically meaningful reduction in migraine days. These domains are not incorporated into the frequency endpoint and therefore cannot be inferred reliably from the responder classification alone.

The reviewed literature also indicates that several additional measures can provide information complementary to MMD and MHD. Acute medication days quantify the frequency with which patients require symptomatic treatment. Measures of attack severity and duration characterise the intensity and temporal extent of individual attacks. MIDAS and MSQ provide information on disability and health-related quality of life, while the MIBS-4 addresses interictal burden [7,16,18]. Work productivity instruments such as the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment questionnaire provide a further distinction between absenteeism and presenteeism.

From a measurement perspective, migraine-day frequency therefore remains an appropriate core outcome for preventive treatment studies because it is reproducible, clinically interpretable and directly responsive to treatment. However, a comprehensive assessment of treatment benefit requires additional outcomes capable of capturing disability, quality of life, productivity, acute medication use and interictal burden. The evidence reviewed in the preceding sections supports the need for such multidimensional assessment without implying that the conventional migraine-day endpoint should be replaced (Table 6).

path: 3.8. Treatment-Related Reduction in Migraine Days and Patient-Reported Outcomes
sections.text:
The reviewed evidence indicates that preventive treatment can reduce the frequency of migraine days while also producing measurable changes in patient-reported disability, quality of life and functional burden. These outcomes are related but distinct, supporting the use of complementary endpoints when evaluating the clinical consequences of preventive therapy.
