Contextual evidence from retrospective surveillance and case ascertainment. Three studies primarily evaluated AI/ML-assisted postoperative SSI surveillance or case ascertainment rather than conventional prediction of a future complication [36,37,38]. Sohn et al. used a Bayesian-network approach to detect clinically important colorectal SSI, achieving an AUROC of 0.827 compared with 0.719 for logistic regression [36]. Cho et al. reported an AUROC of 0.963 for colon-SSI surveillance; at 95% sensitivity, PPV was 21.1%, increasing to 28.9% with rule-based screening, while the estimated manual chart-review workload was reduced by 83.9% [37]. Celik et al. similarly evaluated postoperative colon-SSI surveillance using structured EHR data together with NLP-derived clinical-note features [38]. These studies were retained as contextual evidence relevant to automated surveillance and case finding; their performance was not interpreted as evidence of clinically actionable pre-event prediction unless prediction before outcome onset or a clinically meaningful lead time was demonstrated.

Procedure-specific analyses included trauma laparotomy, where Cobler-Lichter et al. reported AUROCs 0.805 overall, 0.832 for organ-space SSI, and 0.776 for deep SSI [22], and a 2,882,526-operation cohort in which Al Mamlook et al. reported AUROC 0.8518 for a deep neural network under 10-fold cross-validation [40]. Ruan et al.’s GRU-D longitudinal model showed that performance and predictor contribution changed with infection type and postoperative time [42].

Overall, infection/SSI studies addressed clinically distinct tasks ranging from perioperative risk prediction to dynamic postoperative prediction or early detection and retrospective surveillance/case ascertainment. Reported discrimination therefore could not be interpreted without considering predictor timing, outcome definition, intended use, and validation strategy. Surveillance performance and reductions in manual chart-review burden were treated as operational case-finding outcomes rather than evidence of pre-event clinical warning. Among predictive models, interpretation emphasized temporal ordering of predictors and outcomes, validation strategy, calibration, and clinically useful lead time rather than peak AUROC alone.

Eight studies predicted anastomotic/gastrointestinal leakage after colorectal, gastric, esophagogastric, or bariatric surgery, using preoperative, perioperative, or early postoperative information [6,10,23,43,44,45,46,47]. Adams and Papagrigoriadis’ small colorectal neural-network study (n = 76) achieved internal AUC 0.89, sensitivity 85.0%, specificity 82.1%, with 83.3% specificity in a 12-patient prospective pilot [43]. In four Swiss centers, Taha-Mehlitz et al. reported random forest AUC 0.78 internally but 0.60 externally; logistic regression was more stable at 0.69 and 0.61 [44].

Ochs et al. analyzed 9120 colorectal resections using a cross-attention meta-model, which achieved an AUC of 0.89 (95% CI 0.83–0.95) in cross-validation and 0.78 in external validation [6]. Martin-Arevalo et al.’s 24 h postoperative inflammatory model achieved an AUC of 0.819 in development and was subsequently evaluated in a prospective temporal-validation cohort of 250 patients, in which seven anastomotic leaks occurred (2.8%; non-event prevalence 97.2%) [10]. At the prespecified probability threshold of 0.1258, the model achieved an AUROC of 0.73 (95% CI 0.54–0.92), sensitivity of 57.1%, specificity of 60.1%, positive predictive value of 4.0%, and negative predictive value of 97.9%, with three of the seven leaks missed. The reported calibration slope was 0.987, the calibration intercept was approximately 0.505, and the Brier score was approximately 0.094; decision-curve analysis showed positive net benefit across thresholds of approximately 5–20%. The high negative predictive value should be interpreted against the baseline non-event prevalence of 97.2% and therefore does not alone establish strong rule-out performance. Although the calibration slope was close to one, the positive calibration intercept indicates systematic underestimation of risk; calibration should therefore not be described as near ideal.

After gastrectomy, Shao et al. reported random forest AUC 0.89 with sensitivity 81.8% and specificity 82.2% and implemented a web tool [45]; Liu et al. reported SVM AUROC 0.89 versus 0.86 for postoperative-day-4 CRP alone [46]. In 4228 esophageal and 2199 gastric resections, van Kooten et al. found no significant ML advantage: generalized linear regression achieved AUC 0.619 for esophageal leakage and 0.680 after gastrectomy, comparable with neural networks/LASSO/SuperLearner [47]. In 436,807 bariatric procedures, Nudel et al. reported leak AUCs 0.75 for ANN, 0.70 for XGBoost, and 0.63 for logistic regression [23].

Overall, several internally evaluated models approached AUC 0.90 [43,45,46], but external performance could fall substantially [6,44]. The temporally validated 24 h model retained moderate discrimination, but its high negative predictive value occurred in a cohort with a 97.2% non-event prevalence, while the positive calibration intercept indicated systematic risk underestimation despite a calibration slope close to one [10]; conventional regression matched or exceeded ML in the large esophagogastric cohort [47]. Pre/perioperative risk prediction and early postoperative detection were therefore interpreted as distinct tasks.

Five studies evaluated POPF after pancreaticoduodenectomy using preoperative CT/clinical data, perioperative variables, or serial postoperative measurements [7,48,49,50,51]. Kambakamba et al.’s proof-of-principle case–control study (55 POPF/55 controls) reported CT-texture AUC 0.95, sensitivity 96%, and specificity 98% versus risk-score AUCs 0.76 and 0.72, but only 10-fold cross-validation [48]. Lee et al. (n = 1333) combined clinical/body-composition data with CT deep learning; in a temporal holdout, the ensemble achieved AUC 0.75 (95% CI 0.71–0.80) for any POPF and 0.68 (0.58–0.78) for clinically relevant POPF [7].

Han et al. (n = 1769; 221 events) reported maximum AUC 0.74 for a neural network with recursive feature elimination and implemented a web platform, but without independent validation [49]. Shen et al. (n = 2421; 424 grade B/C events) used postoperative information; CatBoost achieved mean AUC 0.81 (95% CI 0.80–0.82) in repeated cross-validation and about 0.83 in random test sets, with early drain-fluid amylase the dominant feature [50].

In the largest cohort, Ingwersen et al. analyzed 4912 patients from 16 Dutch centers (799 clinically relevant POPF) and found near-equivalent bootstrap-validated performance: gradient boosting AUROC 0.74 (IQR 0.73–0.74), Brier 0.13, versus logistic regression AUROC 0.73, Brier 0.12 [51].

Accordingly, the highest discrimination arose from a small internally validated imaging study, whereas larger models generally achieved AUCs around 0.68–0.83 [7,48,49,50]. Postoperative information improved early-diagnostic performance [50], and complex ML did not clearly outperform logistic regression in the largest multicenter cohort [51]. Pre/perioperative risk prediction and postoperative early diagnosis were therefore considered separately.

Two studies modeled broader composite postoperative complications and were analyzed separately because their endpoints combined infectious and noninfectious events [52,53]. Zeng et al. studied 175 liver-resection patients (58 complications): a C5.0 tree achieved AUC 0.91 (95% CI 0.77–1.00), accuracy 92.45%, sensitivity 87.5%, and specificity 94.59%, while random forest had the most favorable decision-curve profile; operative duration, BMI, and incision length were prominent predictors [52].

Hong et al. developed models for serious 30-day complications after laparoscopic radical gastrectomy in 998 patients across 16 centers and externally validated them in 398 patients. The composite included leakage, pulmonary/abdominal infection, wound complications, obstruction, bleeding, pancreatic fistula, sepsis, and other events [53]. Random forest performed best overall: AUC 0.897 development/0.752 external for total gastrectomy and 0.885/0.903 for distal gastrectomy [53].

Thus, broad-complication discrimination ranged from moderate to high, but the liver-resection estimate came from a small internally split cohort whereas gastrectomy underwent independent external validation [52,53]. Because these were heterogeneous composites, they were kept separate from outcome-specific sepsis, infection, leakage, and POPF models.

Validation approaches varied substantially across studies. Fifteen of 45 studies (33.3%) provided a strict temporal, geographic/external-center, or independent-investigator evaluation of the principal model, whereas the remaining studies relied predominantly on internal splitting, cross-validation, bootstrap resampling, or other non-independent evaluation strategies. External performance was not uniformly preserved. Shu et al. declined from an AUROC of 0.892 in internal testing to 0.782 in external validation [1], whereas the intestinal-obstruction model showed external AUROCs ranging from 0.863 to 0.926 across individual and merged external evaluations [2]. The liver-transplant random forest showed similar discrimination in internal and temporal validation (0.731 vs. 0.755) [27], and GloSSI remained relatively stable between derivation and external validation (0.738 vs. 0.730) [5]. In contrast, the Taha-Mehlitz random forest declined from 0.78 internally to 0.60 externally [44], and the Martin-Arevalo model declined from 0.819 in development to 0.73 (95% CI 0.54–0.92) in temporal validation [10].

Explicit calibration analysis was reported in 9 of 45 studies (20.0%), while 12 of 45 (26.7%) provided any calibration-related information. Reported calibration measures included calibration plots, calibration intercepts or calibration-in-the-large, slopes, and observed-to-expected comparisons. For example, GloSSI showed an external calibration intercept of −0.098 and slope of 1.008 [5], whereas Martin-Arevalo reported a slope of 0.987 with an intercept of approximately 0.505 [10]. Ghabisha et al. demonstrated appreciable calibration departures despite high discrimination [4]. Brier scores were considered separately as measures of overall probabilistic prediction error rather than calibration alone; for example, the intestinal-obstruction model reported a Brier score of 0.108 [2], while the temporally validated Martin-Arevalo model reported a Brier score of approximately 0.094 [10].

Decision-curve analysis or another net-benefit assessment was reported in 7 of 45 studies (15.6%). These analyses provided information beyond discrimination by evaluating whether model-based decisions could offer net benefit across clinically relevant probability thresholds. However, no study (0/45) provided a prospective model-guided impact evaluation demonstrating that use of the model changed clinical management, patient outcomes, or resource utilization. Some studies reported operational or implementation-oriented features, including reduction in manual review burden [37] and web-based calculators [45,49], but such tools were not considered evidence of prospective clinical impact. Overall, model maturity was therefore interpreted using independent or temporal validation, calibration, probabilistic performance, threshold-dependent performance, and decision-analytic evidence rather than AUROC alone.

Predictors spanned demographics/comorbidity, laboratory and inflammatory markers, physiological status, operative characteristics, longitudinal postoperative observations, EHR variables, and imaging features. Selection/interpretation methods included regularization, recursive feature elimination, algorithm-derived importance, and SHAP; because definitions, timing, and importance measures were not standardized, predictor effects were synthesized qualitatively by clinical domain and perioperative stage.

For sepsis, recurrent features reflected baseline reserve, inflammation, and perioperative physiological disturbance: albumin, ASA class, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, age, glucose [1]; age, ASA, severity measures, shock index, and fluid variables [2]; transfusion, blood loss, anesthesia duration, bilirubin, fluids, and urine output after liver transplantation [27]; and dynamic respiratory rate, systolic pressure, and heart-rate changes before Sepsis-3 criteria [26]. Infection/SSI models similarly emphasized operative complexity, comorbidity, ASA status, emergency surgery, obesity, and physiological burden [4,40], with trauma-specific injury/transfusion features [22] and colorectal hematologic, inflammatory, renal, and operative variables [32,39].

Postoperative surveillance increasingly relied on evolving information: serial wound and physiological observations [19], NLP-derived SSI terms plus structured recovery variables [38], and longitudinal measurements approaching infection onset [35,42]. Early leak models emphasized platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, monocytes, systemic inflammatory indices, CRP, operative duration, and approach [10], or CRP, albumin, NLR, and immunonutritional indices after gastric surgery [46], whereas purely preoperative leak models used baseline patient/procedural factors [6,44].

POPF prediction was more anatomical and procedure specific, repeatedly using duct diameter, gland texture, BMI, albumin, operative characteristics, and CT-derived pancreatic/body-composition features [7,48,49]; with postoperative data, drain-fluid amylase became dominant while duct size, tumor size, and texture remained relevant [50]. Across outcomes, preoperative models emphasized baseline reserve and inflammation, perioperative models procedural burden and physiology, and postoperative models dynamic inflammatory, wound, physiological, or drain signals [1,19,27,50]. No single predictor set dominated across all populations or outcomes.

Clinical and methodological heterogeneity remained substantial in population, outcome and definition, prediction horizon/timing, data modality, model development, validation stage, and performance metric. Primary sepsis-related studies differed not only in prediction timing but also in endpoint ascertainment, ranging from Sepsis-3-defined postoperative events to ICD-coded or SIRS-based sepsis/septic-shock definitions and a qSOFA-based proxy; prediction tasks ranged from preoperative risk estimation to dynamic forecasting shortly before Sepsis-3 onset [1,2,3,20,26,27]; infection studies included composite infection and multiple SSI definitions from baseline prediction to longitudinal surveillance [4,19,22,30]; leakage spanned colorectal, gastric, esophagogastric, and bariatric procedures [10,23,44,47]; and POPF varied by target and whether predictors were imaging, perioperative, or postoperative [7,48,49,50]. Reporting also mixed AUROC, classification metrics, AUPRC, F1, Brier/calibration, and net benefit across development, internal, temporal, and external validation stages [5,6,9,53], often with correlated algorithms from the same cohort.

No subgroup therefore met the prespecified comparability criteria for quantitative pooling. Pooled AUROC, sensitivity, specificity, or summary ROC estimates were not calculated because combining internal with external validation or preoperative risk models with postoperative early-warning models would merge clinically distinct tasks. Results were synthesized narratively by outcome, prediction timing, data modality, and validation strategy, emphasizing preservation of performance in temporal/external validation and the presence of calibration or decision-analytic assessment [1,5,9,10].

Narrative sensitivity analyses were undertaken to examine whether the principal interpretation changed under progressively more restrictive evidence definitions. Restriction to studies reporting abdominal/general-surgery-specific performance retained 38 of 45 studies, and the overall interpretation was unchanged. Restriction to genuine pre-event prognostic prediction or postoperative early-warning evaluations likewise retained 38 of 45 studies and did not materially alter the findings.

Within the six primary sepsis-related studies, exclusion of the qSOFA-based proxy study retained five of six studies and did not change the overall interpretation that predictive performance was promising but heterogeneous and incompletely validated. Restriction further to evidence based on strict Sepsis-3 outcome definitions yielded four studies or evaluation cohorts [1,2,26,27]; this substantially narrowed the evidence base but did not alter the cautious conclusion regarding clinical readiness.

When the synthesis was restricted to models undergoing strict temporal, geographic/external-center, or independent-investigator evaluation, 15 of 45 studies remained. Transportability continued to vary, with some models maintaining discrimination and others showing appreciable performance deterioration outside their development setting. Restriction to the eight studies judged at low overall model-evaluation risk of bias using PROBAST + AI resulted in a substantially smaller evidence base but supported the same cautious interpretation. Conversely, exclusion of the 10 studies judged at high evaluation risk of bias retained 35 of 45 studies and did not materially alter the overall conclusions. Detailed study-level inclusion in each sensitivity analysis and linked-cohort considerations are provided in Supplementary Table S5.

path: 3.8. Reporting Bias and Certainty of Evidence
sections.text:
Because no outcome domain contained at least 10 sufficiently comparable studies for quantitative synthesis, funnel plots and regression-based tests for small-study effects were not performed. Publication or reporting bias was therefore considered not formally assessable for all four graded outcome domains and was not assumed to be absent.

Using the protocol-specified GRADE principles operationalized for prediction-model evidence as described in Section 2.9, certainty in predictive performance and transportability was judged very low for primary postoperative sepsis/septic-shock prediction, low for postoperative infection/surgical-site infection, very low for anastomotic leakage, and very low for postoperative pancreatic fistula.

For primary sepsis/septic-shock prediction, risk of bias was judged serious because the six principal studies included three evaluations at low, two at unclear, and one at high overall PROBAST + AI evaluation risk of bias. Inconsistency was serious because outcome definitions, prediction timing, clinical tasks, validation strategies, and reported performance varied substantially. Indirectness was also serious: the evidence included consensus Sepsis-3 outcomes alongside ICD-coded or older SIRS/ACS-NSQIP definitions and a qSOFA-based proxy, and restriction to strict Sepsis-3 evidence reduced the evidence base to four studies or evaluations. Imprecision was serious because several clinically important validation estimates were based on relatively few events or had wide confidence intervals, despite some larger development datasets.

For postoperative infection/SSI, risk of bias was serious because only two of 19 principal evaluations were judged at low overall PROBAST + AI evaluation risk of bias, while 13 were unclear and four were high. Inconsistency was serious because studies differed substantially in infection definition, prediction horizon, surveillance versus prognostic use, surgical population, validation design, and observed discrimination. Indirectness was not downgraded at the body-of-evidence level because most studies directly evaluated postoperative infection or SSI in abdominal or general surgical populations, and restriction to abdominal-specific and genuine pre-event evidence did not materially alter the interpretation. Imprecision was not considered serious overall because several large temporal or external validation cohorts provided relatively precise performance estimates, although individual smaller studies remained imprecise.

For anastomotic leakage, risk of bias was serious because none of the eight principal evaluations was judged at low overall evaluation risk of bias; six were unclear and two were high. Inconsistency was serious because models addressed different operations, prediction time points, predictor sets, and validation settings, with materially different discrimination across internal and external evaluation. Indirectness was not considered serious overall because the studies directly evaluated anastomotic or gastrointestinal leakage after abdominal surgery. Imprecision was serious because important external or temporal validations contained few leakage events or wide uncertainty; notably, the prospective temporal validation of the Martin-Arevalo model included seven leaks and yielded an AUROC of 0.73 with a 95% CI of 0.54–0.92.

For postoperative pancreatic fistula, risk of bias was serious because two of five principal evaluations were high risk, two were unclear, and only one was low risk. Inconsistency was serious because studies differed in the definition of any versus clinically relevant fistula, predictor timing, imaging versus clinical inputs, and model performance. Indirectness was not considered serious overall because all five studies directly addressed pancreatic fistula after pancreatic surgery. Imprecision was serious because independently validated evidence remained sparse, some relevant evaluation cohorts contained relatively few outcome events, and uncertainty around clinically relevant fistula prediction remained substantial.

Five broader postoperative-complication studies in which sepsis was one component of a multisystem or composite prediction framework [21,24,25,28,29] and two additional broad postoperative-complication models [52,53] were retained as contextual evidence but were not assigned separate GRADE certainty ratings. Their reported performance could not be mapped cleanly to one of the four principal outcome-specific claims without combining clinically heterogeneous endpoints. Validation setting and applicability informed the conventional GRADE domains where relevant but were not treated as additional independent downgrading domains. Detailed domain-level judgments are presented in Table 2.

This review of 45 studies found that postoperative AI/ML performance depended at least as much on the clinical prediction task, timing, population, and validation setting as on algorithm choice. Primary sepsis-related models ranged from preoperative risk estimates to dynamic forecasts shortly before onset, and external performance was not uniform: Shu et al. attenuated on independent validation whereas Chen et al.’s intestinal-obstruction model remained comparatively stable [1,2], with liver-transplant studies addressing different prediction windows [26,27].

The same pattern appeared in infection and surgically specific complications. GloSSI retained similar derivation/external discrimination, while PERISCOPE showed cross-hospital variation and benefit from local updating [5,9]; some colorectal leak models deteriorated externally, whereas temporal validation of the early postoperative inflammatory model demonstrated moderate discrimination with a high negative predictive value that required interpretation in the context of the very low event prevalence [10]. These findings reinforce that a high AUROC must be interpreted in relation to where, when, and in whom it was estimated. The principal interpretation remained unchanged in narrative sensitivity analyses restricted to abdominal-specific populations, genuine pre-event prediction or early-warning evaluations, models undergoing temporal, geographic/external-center, or independent evaluation, and studies remaining after exclusion of evaluations judged at high risk of bias.

Greater algorithmic complexity also did not consistently improve clinically relevant performance. Gradient boosting and logistic regression were nearly equivalent for clinically relevant POPF [51], conventional regression matched or exceeded several ML approaches in esophagogastric surgery [47], and complex SSI models did not always retain their development advantage externally [5]. Model value therefore reflects discrimination, calibration, generalizability, predictor availability, interpretability, and the consequences of acting on a prediction rather than an ‘AI versus statistics’ distinction.

Finally, the evidence formed a temporal continuum: preoperative models estimate baseline susceptibility, perioperative models add operative burden and physiological disturbance, and dynamic postoperative models incorporate evolving physiological, inflammatory, wound, or drain information [10,19,26,50]. Later models may discriminate better because they observe information closer to the event. The most mature studies extended beyond internal discrimination to temporal/external validation, calibration, and net-benefit assessment [1,5,9,10], but the available evidence remained insufficient to support routine AI/ML model use across major abdominal surgical populations.

path: 4.2. Prediction Timing and the Clinical Role of AI
sections.text:
Clinical value depends on when a prediction is available relative to the complication. Preoperative, perioperative, and dynamic postoperative models answer different questions, use different information, and provide different windows for action. Preoperative models use demographics, comorbidities, laboratories, nutritional/inflammatory status, and planned procedure characteristics to support counseling, optimization, prevention, and surveillance planning [1,4,7,44], but cannot capture operative complexity, blood loss, transfusion, instability, or the early response to surgery.

Perioperative models add operative duration, blood loss, transfusion, fluid balance, procedural complexity, and intraoperative physiology [2,27,45,51], potentially informing immediate postoperative disposition or monitoring. Dynamic models move closer to the event: physiological trajectories forecast liver-transplant sepsis [26], serial wound/physiological data improved SSI detection [19,42], inflammatory markers informed early leak prediction [10], and drain-fluid amylase became dominant for clinically relevant POPF [50].

This creates an accuracy-lead-time trade-off. Later models may discriminate better because early manifestations are already emerging, but leave less time for intervention; earlier models may be less accurate yet offer more opportunity for prevention, intensified surveillance, diagnostic work-up, or escalation. This distinction is particularly important for SSI, leakage, and fistula: they are not sepsis, but earlier recognition may identify pathways preceding intra-abdominal infection and systemic deterioration.

Future studies should therefore prespecify prediction time, horizon, intended action, and minimum clinically useful lead time, and report performance at clinically meaningful time points. A sequential strategy that updates risk from preoperative stratification through perioperative reassessment to dynamic postoperative warning [9,26,42,50] may better reflect evolving postoperative risk than a single static estimate.

path: 4.3. Validation, Calibration, and Translation to Clinical Utility
sections.text:
A major translational gap was the reliance on internal validation. Cross-validation, bootstrap resampling, and random splits estimate performance within the available data but do not establish transportability. Several models changed materially in independent or temporal populations [1,10,44,53], whereas others retained broadly similar performance across external or temporal cohorts, including the intestinal-obstruction model, the liver-transplant random forest, and GloSSI [2,5,27]. Transportability must therefore be demonstrated rather than inferred.

PERISCOPE further showed that external validation may lead to local updating: performance differed across hospitals and improved after adaptation to local historical data [9]. Because case mix, coding, laboratory workflows, procedure mix, and prevalence differ by institution, recalibration or updating may be necessary, but any adapted model requires renewed validation.

Calibration is distinct from discrimination and was less consistently reported. GloSSI showed close external calibration, whereas highly discriminative gastrointestinal SSI models demonstrated appreciable calibration departures [4,5]. The temporally validated colorectal-leak model reported a calibration slope close to one, but its positive calibration intercept indicated systematic underestimation of risk, illustrating why slope and intercept should be interpreted jointly rather than describing calibration as near ideal [10]. Thus, good ranking does not guarantee probabilities suitable for threshold-based decisions. Decision-curve analyses in selected studies estimated potential net benefit [1,4,9,10], but analytical utility is not evidence that implementation improves outcomes; likewise, a web calculator demonstrates accessibility, not impact [45,49].

Operational evidence was limited but informative: ML-assisted SSI surveillance improved PPV and reduced estimated chart-review workload [37]. Clinical translation should therefore progress from internal validation to temporal/external validation, calibration, decision-threshold and workflow assessment, and ultimately prospective impact studies testing whether model-guided care changes management, outcomes, or resource use.

path: 4.4. Predictor Patterns, Interpretability, and Model Complexity
sections.text:
Predictive information was multidimensional, spanning physiological reserve, comorbidity, inflammatory/nutritional status, operative burden, and evolving postoperative physiology. Primary sepsis-related models repeatedly selected albumin, ASA status, inflammatory indices, age, glucose, transfusion/blood loss, fluid balance, and vital-sign trajectories [1,26,27]. Predictor importance shifted with timing: preoperative models emphasized baseline patient/procedure data [1,32,33,44], perioperative models operative burden and physiology [2,27,45,51], and postoperative models serial physiological, wound, inflammatory, and drain-derived data [10,19,42,50].

Procedure-specific anatomy added further signal in POPF, including duct diameter, gland characteristics, body composition, and CT-derived features [7,48,49]. Such imaging and multimodal inputs may add information but also require standardized acquisition, preprocessing, and validation across scanners and institutions before generalization can be assumed.

Feature-importance methods—including random forest/boosting importance, recursive feature elimination, and SHAP—describe contributions within a specific model and dataset, not causality. Rankings can shift with predictor correlation, missingness, measurement frequency, feature engineering, and institutional practice, as reflected by variation across SSI populations [4,22,39,40]. Reduced predictor sets, feature rankings, and web tools may aid use [38,45,49], but clinically meaningful interpretability also requires knowing when predictors are available, whether probabilities are calibrated, and what action follows a given risk.

More complexity was not inherently better: generalized linear regression matched or exceeded several ML methods in esophagogastric surgery [47], and gradient boosting and logistic regression were almost equivalent for POPF [51]. Although flexible algorithms can capture nonlinearities and interactions that simpler models may miss, added complexity should be justified by demonstrable incremental performance during appropriate validation. Future models should therefore prioritize clinically coherent, reproducibly measured predictors available at the intended decision point and justify dynamic, imaging, NLP, or multimodal inputs through reproducible incremental value over simpler baselines.

path: 4.5. Methodological Limitations of the Current Evidence Base
sections.text:
The evidence base remained methodologically heterogeneous. Many studies were retrospective, single-center, registry based, or derived from routine EHRs, with fewer rigorous temporal or independent external validations [1,4,9,49]. Such datasets enable scale but can encode institution-specific selection, workflows, coding, predictor availability, and outcome ascertainment, so development performance cannot be assumed to generalize.

Sample size alone did not guarantee reliability. Cohorts ranged from small procedure-specific studies to hundreds of thousands or millions of operations [20,23,40], yet rare outcomes could still yield few events; conversely, very high discrimination sometimes came from small cohorts [43,48]. Credibility therefore depends on event counts relative to model complexity, feature-selection stability, and validation rigor.

Outcome ascertainment was heterogeneous even within the primary sepsis-related evidence. Three studies consistently used Sepsis-3 [2,26,27], Shu et al. used ICD-10-coded sepsis/severe sepsis/septic shock during development but Sepsis-3 in external validation [1], Bunn et al. used an older ACS-NSQIP/SIRS-based definition [20], and Fransvea et al. modeled qSOFA ≥ 2 as a proxy endpoint [3]. These definitions should not be interpreted as interchangeable representations of postoperative sepsis. Outcome definitions and prediction targets also varied across composite infection, SSI subtypes, leakage, and fistula. Prediction timing added further heterogeneity because postoperative laboratory, documentation, wound, physiological, and drain data may represent increasingly proximal manifestations of the outcome [10,19,38,50]. Without explicit prediction times/horizons and predictor availability, high performance may reflect near-event detection rather than clinically useful early prediction.

Analytical pipelines differed in missing-data handling, feature selection, class imbalance, preprocessing, hyperparameter tuning, internal validation, and model selection; flexible algorithms and low-event datasets are particularly susceptible to optimism, and testing many algorithms can favor chance winners if development and evaluation are not separated. Reporting was also uneven: AUROC predominated while calibration, uncertainty, precision–recall, and threshold metrics were less consistent. For uncommon or imbalanced outcomes, good discrimination may coexist with low PPV, and overall accuracy may appear favorable despite inadequate sensitivity for the complication of interest [37,38]. These differences, reflected in PROBAST + AI, limited direct comparison and precluded defensible pooling; the main evidence gap is not absence of promising models but insufficiently standardized, independently validated evidence of transportability.

path: 4.6. Clinical Implications and Future Research Priorities
sections.text:
The near-term role of perioperative AI is to support, not replace, clinical judgment through risk stratification, surveillance, and timely escalation at defined points in the surgical pathway. Intended use should be specified before development because preoperative optimization tools and postoperative surveillance systems require different predictors, timing, thresholds, and actions. Models should use information that is reproducibly available at the intended decision point and integrate with routine workflows; SMART, PERISCOPE, and SSI-surveillance studies illustrate potential pathways for perioperative assessment, monitoring/discharge support, and prioritization of manual review [8,9,37,38].

Before adoption, promising models require geographical and temporal external validation, calibration assessment, and transparent local updating when justified. PERISCOPE showed that adaptation could improve local discrimination, calibration, and net benefit [9], whereas GloSSI remained comparatively stable externally [5], indicating that the need for recalibration varies by model and setting.

Prospective evaluation should follow adequate retrospective/external validation. A silent deployment phase can test real-time data availability, technical reliability, workflow fit, alert burden, and live predictive performance before outputs influence care; SMART specifically proposed such an approach [8]. Subsequent impact studies should determine whether risk estimates alter clinician behavior, diagnostic timing, treatment, complications, resource use, or patient-centered outcomes.

Evaluation should also move beyond AUROC to calibration, threshold-specific sensitivity/specificity, predictive values, precision–recall for uncommon outcomes, and decision-analytic measures. Thresholds must reflect the consequences of false positives/negatives and the action triggered; a threshold suitable for chart-review prioritization may be inappropriate for invasive investigation, delayed discharge, or treatment escalation [9,37,38]. Clinical thresholds should be prespecified according to intended use rather than selected retrospectively to maximize reported performance.

Implementation is also a maintenance problem. Changes in populations, surgery, antimicrobials, laboratory workflows, and EHR systems can alter data distributions and prevalence; PERISCOPE explicitly considered performance/data drift [9]. Systems therefore need monitoring, criteria for recalibration/retraining, and validation of revised models. Equity should be assessed through prespecified subgroup discrimination and calibration because acceptable aggregate performance does not ensure comparable performance across patient groups; PERISCOPE’s subgroup analyses also highlighted missing race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic information [9].

Practical deployment also requires explicit local governance and technical oversight. Institutions should define clinical and technical ownership of the model, responsibilities for performance surveillance, criteria for recalibration or retraining, version control, audit trails, and circumstances requiring temporary suspension or retirement of a model. EHR integration should be evaluated for local variable mapping, measurement units, missingness, data latency, interface reliability, and alert routing, because changes in data pipelines or clinical workflows may alter both model inputs and downstream actions. Post-deployment monitoring should therefore include discrimination, calibration, event prevalence, data-quality and performance drift, alert burden, and clinically relevant subgroup performance. Material changes to the model, EHR configuration, or input-data pipeline should prompt documented reassessment and, where appropriate, revalidation before continued clinical use.

Future research should therefore shift from algorithm development toward clinically embedded evaluation with defined time points/horizons and responses, standardized outcomes, comparison with appropriate conventional baselines, multicenter/temporal validation, calibration, prospective workflow testing, and impact studies. Additional complexity from dynamic, imaging, NLP, or multimodal inputs should be justified by reproducible incremental value at a clinically useful time point.

path: 4.7. Strengths and Limitations of This Review
sections.text:
This review’s main strengths were its clinically structured synthesis across primary sepsis-related outcomes, infection/SSI, leakage, POPF, and broader postoperative complications while keeping these outcomes distinct; its interpretation of models within preoperative, perioperative, and dynamic postoperative time points [10,19,26,50]; and its emphasis on validation, calibration, predictor availability, interpretability, and utility rather than headline AUROC alone. External performance was explicitly distinguished from development performance because transportability was preserved in some models but attenuated in others [1,5,9,44]. Avoiding quantitative pooling also prevented clinically distinct populations, outcomes, prediction horizons, and validation stages from being collapsed into misleading summary estimates.

The review also has limitations. Its broad eligibility framework introduced substantial clinical heterogeneity. Clinical sepsis ascertainment itself was heterogeneous, including consensus Sepsis-3 definitions, administrative/coded or older SIRS-based criteria, and a qSOFA-based proxy; consequently, the six primary sepsis-related studies were not treated as methodologically equivalent evidence of the same endpoint. SSI, leakage, and fistula are not surrogate definitions of sepsis; they provide contextual evidence but cannot establish primary sepsis-related prediction performance.

Searches covered PubMed, Scopus, and CENTRAL through 10 August 2026, so studies indexed only elsewhere or published later may have been missed. Because no subgroup was sufficiently comparable for pooling, summary accuracy estimates and conventional publication-bias tests were not produced.

Primary-study reporting was incomplete for calibration, prediction horizons, uncertainty, decision analysis, and threshold metrics, and outcome definitions/validation methods varied. Large registries or routine-care datasets may also overlap, so study sample sizes cannot be summed as unique patients. Finally, the literature predominantly evaluated model development or observational performance rather than prospective model-guided care; this review can therefore appraise predictive performance and methods but cannot establish that implementation improves diagnostic timing, management, outcomes, or resource use.

Accordingly, the review’s contribution is not a pooled estimate of AI performance but a structured appraisal of where perioperative prediction models stand, how their reported performance should be interpreted, and what evidence is still required before routine implementation.

Although selected AI/ML models demonstrated promising discrimination for postoperative sepsis and related complications, the available evidence remains insufficient to support routine AI/ML model use across major abdominal surgical populations. Across the 45 included studies, performance depended substantially on the clinical outcome, surgical population, prediction timing, predictor availability, and validation strategy; high development performance was not consistently maintained during temporal or external evaluation, and greater model complexity did not reliably outperform conventional approaches.

Postoperative infection, anastomotic leakage, and pancreatic fistula should remain distinct from primary sepsis-related prediction, while primary sepsis-related outcomes should be interpreted according to their underlying clinical definitions, ascertainment methods, and prediction tasks. Future models should therefore be anchored to a clearly defined clinical use case, prediction time and horizon, and intended clinical response, followed by rigorous temporal and multicenter external validation, assessment of calibration, and prospective model-guided impact studies. The most clinically valuable perioperative AI model will not necessarily be the one with the highest AUROC, but one that is reliable, calibrated, timely, transportable, interpretable, and demonstrably actionable in real-world surgical care.

title: Intravesical BCG-induced granulomatous prostatitis mimicking prostate cancer in patients with non-muscle invasive bladder cancer: a systematic review

sections.text: PurposeBacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) therapy is a standard-of-care for non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), and granulomatous prostatitis (GP) is a side effect often misdiagnosed as prostate cancer (PCa). We conducted a systematic review to clarify the clinical spectrum of BCG-induced GP.MethodsMEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched in June 2026. We sought studies reporting GP associated with BCG therapy for NMIBC, including case reports and case series. Risk of bias was evaluated using ROBINS-I and JBI tools. Findings were synthesized narratively (CRD420261324758).ResultsForty-seven studies were included, comprising 23 case reports, 19 case series, and 5 comparative studies. In case series, abnormal digital rectal examination findings were reported in 100/240 (42%) evaluable cases. PSA elevation (> 4 ng/mL) occurred in 104/194 (54%) patients but often declined spontaneously during follow-up. Suspicious MRI findings were common, with PI-RADS ≥ 4 lesions reported in 71/82 (87%) cases, whereas biopsy-confirmed PCa was detected only in 12/151 (7.9%) patients. However, Grade Group and definitions of clinically significant PCa (csPCa) were incompletely and inconsistently reported, precluding a reliable estimate of csPCa frequency. Limitations include the predominance of descriptive studies and potential selection bias.ConclusionBCG-induced GP frequently presents with transient PSA elevation and suspicious MRI findings that rarely indicate true PCa. In BCG-exposed patients with elevated PSA or PI-RADS ≥ 4 lesions, structured observation with careful follow-up should be considered before proceeding to immediate biopsy.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s00345-026-06883-3.

Intravesical Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) therapy is a standard-of-care immune treatment for non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) [1–3]. While highly effective, it is associated with several treatment-related adverse events, including the so-called granulomatous prostatitis (GP) [4]. The proposed pathophysiology involves intraprostatic reflux of BCG-containing urine through the prostatic ducts, leading to localized granulomatous inflammatory reactions. The BCG-induced GP remains incompletely characterized in the contemporary multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) era. However, growing clinical observations suggest that it can closely mimic prostate cancer (PCa) via prostate-specific antigen (PSA) elevation and morphologic changes on mpMRI. Consequently, standard PCa diagnostic pathways, including PSA-based assessment and MRI-targeted biopsy strategies, may demonstrate reduced specificity in BCG-exposed patients, potentially leading to unnecessary prostate biopsy (PBx), patient anxiety, financial toxicity [5], and potential overtreatment in those with incidental findings of clinically-insignificant cancer.

Despite these important clinical implications, no comprehensive review has systematically evaluated its clinical presentation and imaging characteristics. In the absence of clear follow-up strategies or standardized diagnostic criteria, clinicians face uncertainty in balancing oncologic vigilance with avoidance of invasive procedures. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review to clarify the clinical spectrum of BCG-induced GP and to provide clinically relevant insights that may help recalibrate PCa workup strategies in BCG-exposed patients while maintaining oncologic safety.
The protocol has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews database (PROSPERO: CRD420261324758).

This systematic review was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2) [6] and adhered to the AMSTAR-2 checklist (Supplementary Appendix 1) [7]. On 24 February 2026, comprehensive literature searches were performed in MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, and the Web of Science Core Collection to identify studies reporting on GP associated with intravesical BCG therapy for NMIBC. An updated search was conducted on 1 June 2026. The complete search strategy is detailed in Supplementary Appendix 2.

The primary objective of this review was to clarify the clinical presentation, imaging characteristics, and histopathological features, and to provide clinically relevant insights to guide appropriate diagnostic evaluation and management. Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts to identify potentially eligible studies, followed by a full-text review of relevant articles. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus with additional co-authors.

We defined the study question using the PECO framework: In adult patients diagnosed with NMIBC (Population), does exposure to BCG therapy (Exposure), compared with patients not treated with BCG where applicable (Comparator), lead to clinical findings that may mimic PCa, including PSA elevation, abnormal digital rectal examination (DRE) findings, imaging abnormalities suggestive of prostate malignancy, and PCa detection rates on PBx (Outcomes). Because the primary aim of this review was descriptive, both comparative and non-comparative studies, including case reports and case series, were considered eligible. Studies without prostate-related evaluation or outcomes were excluded. Articles that did not provide original patient-level data, including review articles, editorials, letters without clinical information, and author replies, were excluded. Conference abstracts without full-text publications were excluded due to insufficient methodological and clinical detail.

Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using a standardized data collection form. For each study, the following information was collected when available: first author’s name, year of publication, country, study design, number of patients, imaging modality, and diagnostic method. Potential cohort overlap was assessed by comparing study institutions, recruitment periods, study populations, and author groups across the included studies.

At the patient level, demographic and treatment-related variables included age, PSA levels before and after BCG therapy, DRE findings, imaging characteristics (including PI-RADS score), and PBx results. For case reports, management approaches (e.g., observation, antibiotics, anti-tuberculous therapy, biopsy, or surgery) and the subsequent clinical course were also documented. Any discrepancies in data extraction were resolved through discussion and consensus between the reviewers.

Risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized comparative studies when applicable [8]. Case reports and case series were assessed using JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist [9]. Two authors independently assessed the RoB for each study. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus with co-authors.

Given the substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity and the predominance of case reports and small case series, findings were synthesized narratively, and available data were summarized using descriptive statistics. Effect measures were not predefined. Reporting bias and certainty of evidence were not formally assessed due to the descriptive nature of data synthesis.

The study selection process is illustrated in Fig. 1. Forty-seven studies were included, comprising 23 case reports [10–32], 19 case series [33–51], and 5 non-randomized comparative studies [52–56]. Four studies were prospective [42, 45, 46, 53], and the remaining studies were retrospective. The overall characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table 1. Detailed patient characteristics for case reports are shown in Supplementary Table 3.

path: Assessment of risk of bias and quality of study
sections.text:
The RoB assessment for each included comparative study is summarized in Supplementary Table 4. Based on the ROBINS-I tool, 3 studies were classified as having a moderate RoB, and 2 as having a serious RoB [52, 54]. The primary source of bias was selection bias, as several studies included only patients undergoing MRI or PBx after BCG therapy, which may not represent the overall BCG-treated population.

The methodological quality assessment of included case reports and case series based on the JBI critical appraisal tools is summarized in Supplementary Tables 5 and 6. Overall, most studies were considered to be of moderate to high quality, with histopathological confirmation and detailed imaging findings generally well reported. However, unclear consecutive patient inclusion and limited longitudinal follow-up were common limitations.

Details of the included case series are presented in Tables 2 and 3, and Supplementary Table 7, while details of the included comparative studies are presented in Table 4. Because not all studies reported all clinical, imaging, pathological, and follow-up variables, the denominators vary across analyses and are reported separately for each outcome where applicable.

Across all included studies, the age of patients with BCG-induced GP ranged from 46 to 88 years, while the median age in studies reporting summary age data ranged from 64 to 74 years. Abnormal DRE findings were reported in 100 of 240 evaluable cases (42%) [35, 39, 42, 44, 46–51]. The indication for DRE varied across studies, from predefined follow-up to evaluation for suspected PCa. Notably, 22 of 36 patients (61%) in the case series with available data were asymptomatic at presentation [33, 39, 43, 48]. Case reports similarly described asymptomatic patients with suspicious DRE findings, often leading to biopsy for diagnostic confirmation.

In the comparative studies, Cabello et al. compared patients undergoing prostate MRI and targeted biopsy for suspected PCa with (n = 20) and without (n = 692) prior BCG exposure. Suspicious DRE findings were more frequent in the BCG-exposed group (30% vs. 19%), although the difference was not statistically significant (exact p-value not reported) [53]. Similarly, Akagi et al. compared BCG-exposed NMIBC patients undergoing PBx with non-BCG-exposed patients undergoing PBx for suspected PCa, and observed a higher proportion of abnormal DRE findings in the BCG-exposed group (n = 22) than in the non- exposed group (n = 28) (45% vs. 39%, p = 0.06) [52].

Among case series reporting PSA data, PSA elevation (≥ 4 ng/mL) was observed in 104 of 194 evaluable patients (54%) [33, 35–37, 39, 40, 43, 44, 46, 47, 51]. Reported PSA levels ranged from 0.6 to 22.9 ng/mL. PSA-related findings were reported in 3 case series [45–47]. Importantly, all case series that assessed PSA levels before and after BCG reported a spontaneous decline in PSA levels without specific treatment. PSA levels generally decreased toward baseline within approximately 3 months, although normalization took up to 6–12 months in some patients, suggesting that BCG-associated PSA elevation is transient and self-limiting (Table 2). Nonetheless, case reports described PSA elevation as a common trigger for further diagnostic evaluation and PBx.

Two comparative studies evaluated PSA levels according to prior BCG exposure. Neither Akagi et al. (5.8 vs. 6.3 ng/mL) nor Cabello et al. (median 6.6 vs. 6.4 ng/mL) found a significant difference between BCG-exposed and non-exposed patients [52, 53].

MRI-related findings were reported in 10 case series [35–44].MRI was generally performed for suspected PCa following PSA elevation and/or abnormal DRE, although some studies obtained MRI for bladder cancer staging or follow-up.

Among case series with reported PI-RADS assessment, PI-RADS ≥ 4 lesions were observed in 71 of 82 cases (87%) [35–42]. Four of these studies reported that MRI alone is insufficient to reliably distinguish GP from PCa [35, 36, 39, 44], while the remaining studies described specific imaging patterns that may help suggest GP. Typical MRI features included diffuse involvement, T1 hyperintensity, and ring enhancement patterns. Most lesions were nevertheless categorized as PI-RADS ≥ 4 (Table 3). Case reports similarly described lesions with suspicious mpMRI findings frequently classified as PI-RADS ≥ 4, often prompting PBx for diagnostic evaluation.

In Cabello et al., 19 of 20 BCG-exposed patients had at least one PI-RADS ≥ 4 lesion. At the lesion level, PCa (ISUP Grade Group [GG] ≥ 1) was detected in 3/18 PI-RADS 4 lesions (16.7%, 95%CI 5.8–39.2%) and 2/9 PI-RADS 5 lesions (22.2%, 95%CI 6.3–54.7%), compared with 61.6% (95%CI 57.3–65.8%) and 90.7% (95%CI 85.0-94.4%), respectively, in non-BCG-exposed patients [53]. Another comparative analysis demonstrated that diffuse morphology and T1 hyperintensity were characteristic MRI features of GP, which may aid in differentiating inflammatory lesions from PCa in selected cases (n = 99) [55]. Kim et al. reported that higher BMI and larger prostate volume were associated with the development of BCG-induced granulomatous lesions on MRI after BCG therapy (n = 194) [56].

Details of the findings from other imaging modalities are presented in Supplementary Table 7. Computed tomography (CT)-related findings were reported in 2 case series [33, 34]. CT was performed as part of oncological follow-up for bladder cancer rather than being specifically prompted by prostate-related symptoms. BCG-related GP was reported to present as prostatic enlargement or low-attenuation lesions with contrast enhancement, occasionally mimicking primary or metastatic tumors. In 1 series, incidental prostate abnormalities were observed in 11 of 38 patients (29%) and resolved spontaneously during follow-up [34].

Ultrasound (US)-related findings were reported in 4 case series [48–51]. On US, hypoechoic lesions were frequently observed, but these findings were generally nonspecific and often indistinguishable from PCa. Despite suspicious imaging findings, no biopsy-confirmed PCa was detected in these studies.

Histopathological confirmation was available in most case series, as the majority of studies included biopsy-proven GP. Among biopsy-confirmed cases, PCa was detected in 12 of 151 patients (7.9%) [33, 35–44, 46, 47, 49–51]. Grade Group was reported for 10 of these cancers: 5 were GG1, 4 were GG2, and 1 was GG5. Information on clinically significant PCa (csPCa) was inconsistently reported, and study-specific definitions were available in only 2 studies. Therefore, the overall frequency of csPCa could not be reliably estimated (Supplementary Table 8).

One comparative study demonstrated that PCa in BCG-exposed patients was detected only when biopsy was performed more than 1 year after treatment, whereas biopsies performed within 1 year showed no malignancy [52]. Hong et al. reported that PCa detection after BCG therapy was associated with bladder tumour location, with lower detection rates in patients with tumours involving the bladder neck or trigone compared with other locations (4.5% vs. 35%, p < 0.001; n = 59) [54].

To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review to comprehensively evaluate the clinical and imaging characteristics of BCG-induced GP, with a particular focus on its potential to mimic PCa. Our findings highlight several key associations. First, PSA elevation (> 4 ng/mL) was observed in 54% of evaluable patients, typically during or shortly after BCG induction, and subsequently declined spontaneously, with normalization occurring within 3–12 months. Second, although certain MRI patterns may suggest GP, PI-RADS ≥ 4 lesions were commonly observed after BCG therapy, with a relatively low rate of PCa detection. Finally, GP and PCa show substantial overlap in both clinical presentation and imaging findings, and histopathological confirmation by biopsy may be required when a definitive diagnosis is necessary.

In the setting of BCG therapy, PSA and mpMRI appear to be less specific for PCa detection. PSA elevation was frequently observed but often declined spontaneously during follow-up. Notably, PSA levels may decline even during maintenance BCG therapy. In a study incorporating maintenance BCG, PSA remained elevated at 3 months but declined by 6 months and approached baseline by 12 months despite ongoing maintenance therapy [46]. However, available evidence is insufficient to define an optimal timing for PSA assessment relative to individual maintenance cycles or a specific interval for deferring PBx. Similarly, suspicious MRI findings were common after BCG therapy, with PI-RADS ≥ 4 lesions frequently reported despite relatively low PCa detection rates. The timing of evaluation may also be relevant. Akagi et al. reported that PCa was identified only in patients undergoing PBx more than 1 year after BCG treatment, whereas biopsies performed within 1 year revealed only granulomatous inflammatory lesions [52]. Together with the observed spontaneous resolution of PSA and MRI abnormalities in several studies, these findings suggest that PSA and MRI abnormalities after BCG therapy may reflect inflammatory changes rather than malignancy.

From a histopathological perspective, BCG-induced GP is characterized by epithelioid granuloma formation with dense inflammatory infiltrates and occasional caseous necrosis. Pathological studies have shown that such lesions may occur more frequently than clinically recognized after intravesical BCG therapy; for example, GP was identified in 75% of cystoprostatectomy specimens from patients previously treated with BCG [57]. However, the interval between BCG exposure and cystoprostatectomy was not reported, limiting interpretation of the duration of these histopathological changes. Furthermore, granulomatous inflammation tends to involve the peripheral zone and follow the prostatic ductal system, suggesting that intraprostatic reflux of BCG-containing urine may contribute to its pathogenesis [58]. These pathological features likely explain why the inflammatory lesions can demonstrate diffusion restriction and enhancement patterns on mpMRI that mimic PCa. Crucially, because this granulomatous inflammation preferentially involves the peripheral zone—the most common location of PCa—BCG-induced GP can generate findings that closely resemble malignancy, thereby substantially reducing the specificity of PI-RADS-based assessment in this patient population.

When interpreting these suspicious prostate findings, the broader clinical context of patients receiving intravesical BCG therapy must be prioritized. These patients typically present with NMIBC, are often of advanced age, and frequently harbour multiple comorbidities. In many instances, the patient’s overall prognosis is primarily dictated by the clinical course of their bladder cancer rather than the presence of concomitant PCa. Therefore, the clinical benefit of detecting incidental, often low-grade PCa must be rigorously balanced against the risks of overdiagnosis and the morbidity associated with invasive procedures. Clinical decision-making in this setting should prioritize the optimal management of the primary bladder malignancy, maintaining a high threshold for aggressive prostate interventions.

Based on the available evidence, a pragmatic approach incorporating the timing of BCG exposure and the evolution of prostate findings may help guide clinical management. Establishing a baseline PSA value before BCG treatment may facilitate subsequent interpretation. Following BCG therapy, transient PSA elevation and suspicious imaging findings should be interpreted in the context of their evolution during follow-up. In the absence of persistent or strongly suspicious findings, structured observation with serial PSA testing and/or follow-up mpMRI may be a reasonable initial approach. PBx should be considered when PSA elevation persists, imaging abnormalities progress or remain suspicious, or other clinical features raise concern for PCa.

This study has several limitations. First, the majority of the included evidence relies on case reports and small case series, which are inherently prone to publication and reporting biases; because studies with striking findings are preferentially published, the overall certainty of evidence remains low. Second, substantial heterogeneity in patient demographics, BCG protocols, and imaging parameters precluded a formal quantitative meta-analysis. Third, many studies focused selectively on patients who underwent PBx or mpMRI due to clinical suspicion, introducing verification bias and potentially overrepresenting suspicious imaging findings. Therefore, the reported PCa detection rates do not reflect the true prevalence of PCa among all BCG-treated patients. Furthermore, Grade Group was incompletely reported, and definitions of csPCa were rarely provided and were not uniform across studies, precluding a reliable estimate of the frequency of csPCa. Finally, the lack of long-term follow-up and prospective comparative data makes it difficult to ascertain the natural history of BCG-induced GP, highlighting the need for well-designed prospective studies to optimize future diagnostic strategies.

BCG-induced GP is an underrecognized condition that can closely mimic PCa. PSA elevation and suspicious MRI findings after BCG therapy may reflect transient inflammatory changes, potentially reducing the specificity of standard PCa diagnostic markers in this population. Therefore, even in BCG-exposed patients presenting with elevated PSA or PI-RADS ≥ 4 lesions, a strategy of structured observation and careful clinical follow-up could be considered before proceeding to immediate PBx, provided there are no persistent or progressing suspicious findings during longitudinal assessment. Such approach may help avoid unnecessary invasive procedures while maintaining oncologic safety.
