title: Association between HPV vaccine-related social media discourse and regional HPV vaccine coverage in China

sections.text: IntroductionChina's human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination rate remains far below World Health Organization (WHO) targets. This study examined whether HPV vaccine discourse on Weibo is associated with regional vaccine coverage in China.MethodsWe collected HPV vaccine–related Weibo posts from January 2022 to December 2022, with additional posts from January 2025 to December 2025 for temporal comparison. We fine-tuned a Chinese-RoBERTa-wwm-ext model to classify post themes, enabling us to identify discourse focuses and distinguish the nature of its association with coverage. Multivariate regression with nested leave-one-out cross-validation was performed to assess the association between Weibo post related variables and regional coverage rates, comparing against models using socioeconomic indicators (economy, education, healthcare, employment).ResultsA total of 29,638 valid posts were included in the primary analysis. Approximately 30% of the posts were related to “vaccine promotion” and “vaccination experiences”, making them the two most frequent themes. Total post volume correlated strongly with HPV vaccine coverage (one-dose: r = 0.869, 95% confidence interval [0.744, 0.936], P < 0.001; three-dose: r = 0.920 [0.840, 0.961], P < 0.001), exceeding all included socioeconomic factors. Total post volume models outperformed socioeconomic models (LOOCV R2: one-dose 0.643 vs 0.606; three-dose 0.818 vs 0.662). After excluding retrospective themes, potentially prospective posts plus socioeconomic factors improved prediction (LOOCV R2: one-dose 0.620 vs 0.593; three-dose 0.797 vs 0.720). In 2025, posts decreased by 48.1% and decline in posts related to Theme 1 was the most pronounced.ConclusionHPV vaccine discourse on Weibo was associated with regional coverage. Social-media signals deliver supplementary information beyond conventional socioeconomic indicators, which could serve as a complementary public-health surveillance tool to identify regional needs and barriers.

Cervical cancer is one of the most prevalent cancers among women, with an estimated 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths worldwide in 2022.1 Its incidence and mortality both rank fourth among all cancers in women. In China, cervical cancer accounts for over 40% of all gynecological cancers, with approximately 110,000 new cases reported in 2022,2 posing a significant threat to women's health. Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a necessary but insufficient cause of cervical cancer, and HPV vaccination can reduce its incidence by around 70%.3, 4, 5 To eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem by 2030, the World Health Organization (WHO) established global targets in 2020,6 which include the mandate that 90% of girls complete the full course of HPV vaccination by the age of 15. The HPV vaccine was first approved by the China Food and Drug Administration (CFDA) in July 2016,7 a decade after Merch's quadrivalent HPV vaccine, Gardasil, received its initial authorization.8 Although the HPV vaccination rate in China has increased from 0.01% in 2017 to 10.15% in 2022,9 it remains relatively low. Among girls aged 9-14, the one-dose coverage is only 4%,9 which is far from the target set by the WHO.

Vaccine coverage is influenced by both healthcare accessibility and public acceptance of vaccines.10 Socioeconomic indicators such as education, poverty, and insurance status largely capture disparities in accessibility and acceptance.11, 12 When sufficient policy and economic support is in place, it becomes particularly crucial to enhance public perceptions of vaccines and address vaccine hesitancy.13 Traditional investigations into vaccine confidence and hesitancy are primarily conducted through offline or online questionnaire surveys. In the Internet era, social media platforms serve as crucial channels for the public to disseminate and access health-related information, as well as to engage in discussions concerning public health matters.14, 15, 16 Additionally, media coverage and discourse significantly influence public attention toward public health issues, and some vaccine-related negative information is likely to undermine public acceptance of vaccines.17, 18 Several studies have analyzed the attitudes of the Chinese public towards the HPV vaccine by examining relevant posts on social platforms, which depicted the general public attitudes from an overall perspective yet without establishing correlations with the regional coverage rates of the HPV vaccine.19, 20 In China, there is significant variation in HPV vaccine coverage across different regions, with the one-dose coverage rate in some western provinces even falling below 5%.9 This constitutes one of the key challenges confronting China's national plan for cervical cancer elimination.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the Chinese public's attention to the HPV vaccine and determined whether vaccine discourse on Weibo was associated with regional HPV vaccine coverage in China. We examined HPV vaccine-related posts on the Weibo platform from two perspectives: discourse volume and discourse themes. We collected posts related to the HPV vaccine from Weibo, and each post was thematically annotated using a fine-tuned deep learning model. With over 500 million registered users, Weibo is one of the most popular social media platforms in China and serves as an important channel for public discussions on health-related topics.21, 22 Subsequently, we constructed multivariate regression models to explore the correlation between posts from different regions and vaccination coverage, while comparing these findings with conventional socioeconomic explanatory variables.

We used “HPV vaccine” (in Chinese) as the keyword to search for posts on Weibo. The platform's retrieval algorithm automatically performed semantic expansion on keywords, returning posts that contain the original terms along with their approximate variants and related subject terms.23 A Python web crawler was employed to scrape the primary data of relevant Weibo posts, including the posting time, the main content of the post, as well as the user ID, IP geolocation, number of fans and gender of the publishers. In the primary analysis of this study, we collected relevant Weibo posts from January 2022 to December 2022. Since publicly available vaccination data are currently updated only through 2022, the Weibo data from this period were used to construct regional vaccine coverage interpretation models. Furthermore, we additionally collected data from the most recent one year period (January 2025 to December 2025) for comparison. Although the latest vaccination information is not available, the changes in public concerns reflected in discussions about the HPV vaccine are also of significant value for guiding vaccine promotion efforts.19 Especially with the gradual market launch of domestically produced HPV vaccines and the progressive approval of male vaccination in recent years,24, 25 it has become particularly important to promptly identify the foci of public concern. During the data preprocessing stage, duplicate posts published by the same publisher and posts without valid IP locations were removed. To improve data relevance and classification effectiveness, URLs and special characters were removed during text preprocessing.26 Long posts were subsequently segmented into shorter text chunks to facilitate downstream deep learning-based theme classification. Text segments that did not contain any keywords from the predefined domain-specific lexicon were considered irrelevant noise and excluded from further analysis.27, 28 The custom dictionary used was jointly compiled by two authors, containing a comprehensive range of keywords related to HPV. Data on HPV vaccine coverage by region were obtained from previously published articles,9 and this study reported HPV vaccination data for Chinese women aged 9-45 years using information from the China Immunization Information System (CIIS) electronic vaccine registry. The system covers all immunization clinics across China, recording information for every vaccine dose, including the vaccination date and the vaccine used. The rate we used was estimated cumulative coverage for one-dose and three-dose HPV vaccination among females aged 9–45 years. This was calculated by dividing the total number of females aged 9–45 years in a given study year who received one-dose or three-dose of the vaccine from 2017 (the time when the HPV vaccination was first available in China) to the study year, by the total number of females aged 9–45 years in the given study year.9 Other socioeconomic data were sourced from China's official statistical yearbooks and reports. Further details are available in the supplementary file.

The researchers designed an annotation framework by reviewing a sample of 1000 posts and drawing on existing literature that analyzes themes in HPV vaccine-related posts on social media.20, 29, 30 Our annotation framework covers the main themes related to HPV vaccine discussions on the Weibo platform, specifically: 1) expectations for vaccination, 2) vaccine-related policies and publicity, 3) experiences and feelings regarding vaccination, 4) issues in the vaccine market such as scalpers and smuggling, 5) difficulties in accessing the vaccine, and 6) popular science related to the vaccine. Detailed information regarding the annotation framework can be seen in Table S1.

Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformers (BERT), proposed by Google in 2018, is a “large” pre-trained natural language processing model that outperformed all models before it on the General Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark.31

Chinese-RoBERTa-wwm-ext is developed based on the RoBERTa architecture. The acronym “wwm” denotes Whole Word Masking, a technique involving the masking of entire words.32, 33 This approach enables the model to achieve a more robust comprehension of contextual nuances and semantic relationships, thereby enhancing the accuracy and performance of Chinese text processing tasks.

To deploy the model for analyzing Weibo posts related to HPV vaccines, the pre-trained Chinese RoBERTa-wwm-ext model was fine-tuned using our manually annotated dataset of Weibo posts, following the common paradigm of supervised fine-tuning for downstream text classification tasks. After two researchers (Wang ZW, and Li B) independently annotated the posts and compared their results, followed by a discussion with a third researcher (Wu JY) to resolve discrepancies, we manually annotated 2000 randomly selected posts. Given the relatively small number of posts annotated for Theme 4, we employed stratified sampling based on Theme 4, with 20% of the posts allocated to the test set and 80% used for model training. To enhance the stability and generalization ability of the model, we employed a five-fold cross-validation method and integrated the models using majority voting (based on the prediction results from more than half of the models to determine the annotation).34, 35 The Chinese-RoBERTa-wwm-ext model was used to predict annotations in the test set, and the model predictions were compared with manually generated human annotations. Human annotations were regarded as the ground truth (gold standard), which is a common practice in supervised machine learning and natural language processing studies.

F1 score and precision are widely used evaluation metrics in natural language processing and machine learning studies for assessing classification model performance. They are calculated as follows.F1score=2*11precision+1recallWhere,precision=TruePositiveTruePositive+FalsePositiverecall=TruePositiveTruePositive+FalseNegative

We constructed multivariate regression models to examine the association between Weibo post volume and theme across different regions and vaccine coverage rates, and compared the results with models incorporating socioeconomic explanatory variables. All multivariable models were adjusted for HPV vaccine coverage prior to the study period to control for baseline vaccination levels. Since Theme 3-related posts originated from vaccinated individuals and Theme 4-related posts had an ambiguous relationship with the posters’ vaccination status, we constructed three models for any analyses based on post volume or themes. These models corresponded to three subsets: all posts, posts excluding Theme 3 and Theme 4, and posts excluding Theme 3. This approach allowed us to independently examine the association between potentially prospective posts and vaccine coverage. The number of Weibo posts from different regions was standardized according to the local internet user population. The socio-economic indicators under consideration include GDP (gross domestic product) per capita, health expenditure per capita, out-of-pocket share of health expenditure, proportion of population with tertiary education, unemployment rate, and number of community health service centers. We used a nested leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) procedure in which variable selection was performed within each training fold. In each fold, candidate predictors were first screened by univariable analysis, and those with P < 0.1 were advanced to a multivariable model. We then iteratively removed the predictor with the highest variance inflation factor (VIF) until all retained predictors had VIF < 10. In addition, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using a more stringent VIF cutoff of 5. Retention frequency of each candidate predictor was recorded across all folds, and predictors retained in more than half of the folds were included in the final model. Model performance was quantified using the LOOCV R2, calculated from out-of-fold predictions. All analyses were conducted in R.4.3.3 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria).

A total of 61,384 posts were retrieved using “HPV vaccine” as the search keyword during the period from January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2022. After a preliminary review of the content from the scraped posts, we identified a series of homogeneous posts originating from fans of an idol. These posts contain the hashtag “HPV vaccine”, but the content was entirely unrelated to the vaccine. Consequently, they were excluded from the dataset (N = 8603). For posts with identical content posted by the same poster, only the initial post was retained, while the others were excluded (N = 1074). Posts from users with hidden IP addresses and those originating from countries or regions outside our target 31 provinces were excluded (N = 18,505). Additionally, after filtering the text segments using a custom dictionary, 3564 posts containing no valid content were removed. Finally, 29,638 out of the original 61,384 posts were retained, originating from across 31 provinces (Fig. S1). The fine-tuned model achieved a macro F1 score of 0.8530 and a micro F1 score of 0.8562, indicating effective classification capability and balanced performance across all categories. In the test set, when evaluated against six categories annotation framework, the deep learning model achieved a precision ranging from 79.7% to 90.2%. The detailed performance of the model on each theme can be found in Table 1.Table 1Theme annotation categories for posts related to “HPV Vaccine” on Weibo platform, January 2022 to December 2022.Annotation categoryaDefinitionPerformance of ensemble deep learning modelbF1-scorePrecisionTheme1This post expresses the expectation for HPV vaccination.0.8370.797Theme2This post refers to the policies, programmes, or publicity related to HPV vaccination.0.8950.902Theme3This post refers to the experiences and feelings about HPV vaccination, including side effects.0.8460.897Theme4This post refers to the chaos in the HPV vaccine market, such as scalpers and smuggling.0.8650.889Theme5This post is related to HPV vaccine access, including issues such as lottery systems, long waiting times, and high costs.0.8150.846Theme6This post refers to the dissemination of knowledge related to the HPV vaccine.0.8610.840HPV: human papillomavirus.aEach post can be annotated with multiple themes or not belong to any theme.bPerformance of ensemble deep learning models was assessed by comparing their annotations with annotations made by humans, with human annotation as the gold standard.

Overall, discussions regarding the HPV vaccine on the Weibo platform were predominantly centered on personal experiences and feelings regarding HPV vaccination (Theme 3), with 30.69% (9096/29638) of posts being related to this theme. In addition, those related to other themes included vaccination policy and publicity (Theme 2, 27.75%), popular science on vaccine-related knowledge (Theme 6, 19.37%), expectations for vaccination (Theme 1, 12.92%), complaints about long queues and high costs (Theme 5, 10.57%), and concerns about the vaccine market (Theme 4, 5.74%). The coverage of HPV vaccines in China exhibits a pronounced regional imbalance, generally following a trend of higher coverage in the eastern regions and lower coverage in the western regions. This disparity in vaccine coverage is also echoed by discussions about HPV on social media platforms (Fig. 1A and B). In provinces with leading vaccination rates, such as Beijing and Shanghai, knowledge popularization related to vaccines constitutes the most prevalent theme on the Weibo platform. In contrast, provinces with lower vaccination coverage tend to focus more on Theme 2 and Theme 3 (Fig. 2).Fig. 1Number of HPV Vaccine-Related Weibo posts per region (January 2022 to December 2022) and HPV vaccine (A: one-dose, B: three-dose) coverage rate among women aged 9–45 years in 2022.Fig. 2Proportion of Weibo posts related to each theme, by region.

In the univariate analysis, regardless of the theme, the number of vaccine-related posts exhibited a significant correlation with regional vaccine coverage. Moreover, both the one-dose rate and the three-dose rate (one-dose: r = 0.869, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.744, 0.936], P < 0.001; three-dose: r = 0.920 [0.840, 0.961], P < 0.001) showed the strong correlation with the total number of posts, and this correlation was stronger than that observed for any socioeconomic factor (Table 2). For themes, the volume of posts related to Theme 3 exhibited the strongest correlation with vaccination coverage (one-dose: r = 0.895 [0.792, 0.949], P < 0.001; three-dose: r = 0.942 [0.883, 0.972], P < 0.001). Upon excluding Theme 3, or both Theme 3 and Theme 4, the correlation between the volume of potentially prospective posts and vaccine coverage decreased to some extent, and its association with one-dose coverage was no longer stronger than that with per-capita GDP. Details of the univariate models are presented in Supplementary Table S2. Results of the multivariate models are shown in Table 3. Similar to the findings from univariate analysis, the model constructed based on post volume better out-of-sample model performance for regional coverage across total Weibo posts compared with the model built on socioeconomic factors (LOOCV R2:one-dose 0.643 vs 0.606; three-dose 0.818 vs 0.662). However, when potentially prospective posts are considered, the generalizability of the model deteriorates, and it no longer exhibits advantages for the one-dose vaccination (Table 3). It is worth noting that, in the full model accounting for both post-related variables and socioeconomic factors, model performance improved after excluding Theme 3 and Theme 4 (LOOCV R2:one-dose 0.620 vs 0.593; three-dose 0.797 vs 0.720), and a similar result was observed when only Theme 3 was excluded (LOOCV R2:one-dose 0.608 vs 0.593; three-dose 0.734 vs 0.720). Furthermore, after excluding Theme 3 and Theme 4, the full model constructed with potentially prospective posts and socioeconomic factors (LOOCV R2: one-dose = 0.620; three-dose = 0.797) outperformed From January 2025 to December 2025, a total of 31,865 original posts were retrieved, representing a decrease of 48.1% compared to three years earlier (from Janrary 2022 to December 2022). Among them, the proportions of posts from male users (54.24% vs. 35.20%, χ2 = 3126.6, P < 0.001) and from influential users (50.84% vs. 37.19%, χ2 = 1606.8, P < 0.001) both increased significantly. After screening, a total of 21,767 posts were included for theme annotation using the deep learning model (Fig. S1). Except for the number of posts related to Theme 6, which increased compared to three years earlier, the numbers of posts related to the other themes all decreased to varying degrees (Fig. 3). Among them, the decline in posts related to Theme 1 was the most pronounced, amounting to only 7.86% of the level observed three years ago.Fig. 3Comparison of HPV vaccine-related posts on the weibo platform in 2022 and 2025.

In this study, we leveraged a large-scale social media dataset from Weibo and a fine-tuned deep learning model to systematically examine the relationship between public discourse on the HPV vaccine and regional vaccination coverage in China. Our findings suggest that HPV vaccine-related discourse on Weibo was associated with regional HPV vaccine coverage in China, especially for three-dose coverage. However, the association differed by discourse theme and by vaccination outcome, requiring cautious interpretation.

Posts describing vaccination experiences and feelings are generated after vaccination. Their strong correlation with coverage is expected and should not be interpreted as prospective signal for vaccination or evidence that experience-sharing drives vaccination. In contrast, theme 1, themes 5 and 6 are more directly prospective in nature, whereas may capture unmet needs or informational demand. When analyses distinguished between these types of themes, the association with coverage persisted but became more modest. This suggests that overall post volume may mix anticipatory signals with retrospective accounts of vaccination activity; theme-specific measures are therefore more informative for interpreting the nature of the association and identifying potentially actionable discourse, even though aggregate volume may still show a stronger out-of-sample association with coverage. The dose-specific pattern also merit attention. For three-dose coverage, theme-based variables showed greater incremental value, whereas they showed poorer performance for one-dose coverage. One possible explanation is that the initiation of the first dose is more affected by price, affordability and availability, whereas completion of the full vaccination schedule may depend more on sustained attention and demand.36 Social media discourse may be more informative about the broader vaccination environment associated with completion of the multi-dose schedule than about initial vaccine uptake.

Although the individual coefficients of some socioeconomic variables were unstable in the full model, likely due to collinearity and limited statistical power, when socioeconomic factors were combined with potentially prospective posts variables, model performance was consistently improved compared with models constructed using either set of factors alone. This pattern supports the view that social media discourse may capture a different dimension of the vaccination environment—public attention, perceived barriers, and informational needs—that structural indicators do not fully measure. Socioeconomic indicators capture structural capacity, whereas social media discourse may capture the population's perceived and communicative response to that environment.37 Their complementary explanatory performance suggests that digital discourse may provide information that is not fully represented by conventional socioeconomic indicators. A recent review describes the dual role of internet-based information and social media: they may increase HPV vaccine awareness and demand, but can also amplify misinformation, hesitancy, and access-related concerns.38 Social media surveillance should not be viewed as a replacement for traditional structural indicators but rather as a real-time, high-resolution lens for understanding the psychosocial and informational barriers that persist even when economic and infrastructural conditions are partially met.39

Geographically, provinces with higher vaccination coverage, such as Beijing and Shanghai, exhibited a greater proportion of posts related to vaccine science popularization, whereas provinces with lower coverage tended to focus more on policies, programmes, and publicity. This may reflect different stages of vaccine rollout. Where cost and access remain limiting, discourse should address policy support, and special offers. Where access is less constrained, discourse may need to sustain demand, promote completion of the full schedule, and counter misinformation. The increasing participation of male posters and influential posters suggests that HPV vaccination is becoming framed as a broader public health issue and concerns all genders. In recent years, a variety of affordable domestic vaccines have become available.40 China has also recently approved HPV vaccination for males. These will bring a great shift in the vaccination landscape.

A reduction in the total number of posts and shifts in their composition reflect a decline in public discussions regarding HPV vaccine on social media. Such discussions have become more focused on vaccine policies and the exchange of vaccine-related knowledge, whereas communication concerning expectations for vaccines, sharing of vaccination experiences, and vaccination-related difficulties have decreased substantially. These may partly reflect the shrinking pool of unvaccinated eligible individuals, improved vaccine availability, or the gradual normalization of HPV vaccination. As coverage data for the later period were unavailable, we could not determine whether these discourse changes precede or predict changes in coverage.

These findings support a cautious role for social media monitoring in public health planning. Social media data may help identify region-specific concerns, unmet demand, access barriers, and informational gaps in near real time. However, they should not be used as a stand-alone measure of vaccine confidence or as a replacement for surveys, and structural indicators. The strengths of social-media monitoring lie in its real-time performance and operability, offering a convenient window to understand public attitudes toward vaccination.

Previous studies have utilized Twitter post data to predict county-level heart disease mortality,41 as well as investigated the association between exposure to Twitter information and HPV vaccine coverage.42, 43 However, these studies were conducted in developed Western countries. China, as a developing country with substantial geographical disparities, still has a HPV vaccine coverage that lags far behind the global average. Our findings support a cautious but potentially useful role for social media monitoring in HPV vaccination surveillance. The main value of such data may not be to replace conventional vaccination coverage surveillance or survey-based measures of vaccine confidence. Instead, social media can provide a relatively timely source of information about what people are discussing, which barriers are salient, and how vaccination-related information needs differ across regions. Our study carries certain public health implications, demonstrating that region-level, theme-specific social media discussion content serves as a supplementary indicator for understanding regional disparities in HPV vaccine coverage in China.

This study has several limitations. First, the ecological and observational design precludes causal inference. The observed associations may reflect vaccination generating social media discussion, social media exposure affecting vaccination behavior, shared underlying determinants, or combinations of these pathways. Second, although nested leave-one-out cross-validation was used, the small number of units limits statistical power and the stability and generalizability of model estimates; the findings and differences in model performance should therefore be regarded as exploratory. Third, Weibo users are not representative of the entire population and may be younger and more urban, potentially limiting generalizability. Fourth, IP-based geographic information may not accurately represent the user's residence or vaccination location. Fifth, post counts were standardized by the provincial internet-user population rather than the population eligible for HPV vaccination, which may affect comparisons across regions. Next, of the socioeconomic indicators, demographic metrics come from the 2020 census, whereas unemployment rates rely on 2021, leading to potential temporal mismatches. Finally, the absence of vaccination coverage data after 2022 prevented us from determining whether changes in discourse between 2022 and 2025 preceded subsequent changes in vaccination coverage. Consequently, the present study should be viewed as evidence of regional association and potential surveillance utility rather than validation of social media as a temporal leading indicator of vaccination uptake.

In conclusion, HPV vaccine-related discourse on Weibo was strongly associated with regional HPV vaccination coverage in China, particularly for three-dose coverage. Social media discourse reflects the regional vaccination environment, but the meaning of this association differs according to whether discourse is retrospective or potentially prospective. After accounting for retrospective discourse, potentially prospective social media signals retained complementary information when considered alongside socioeconomic factors. These findings suggest that social media may provide a useful supplementary lens for understanding regional differences in public attention, information needs, and barriers related to HPV vaccination. Future longitudinal studies integrating temporally aligned social media data, vaccination records, and individual-level survey data are needed to determine whether theme-specific social media signals can reliably anticipate changes in HPV vaccination behavior.

title: From Established Care to Precision Menopause Medicine: A Clinical-Actionability Framework for Contemporary Menopause Management

sections.text: Menopause care now spans established hormone therapy, mechanism-based non-hormonal drugs, behavioural interventions, and emerging microbiome- and biomarker-guided approaches. This state-of-the-art narrative review evaluated which dimensions of personalisation are clinically actionable and which remain hypotheses of precision medicine. A structured PubMed/MEDLINE search (January 2020–July 2026), updated to August 2026 and supplemented by landmark studies, current guidelines, and regulatory sources, was synthesized using a four-tier clinical-actionability framework (A, established; B, evidence-supported off-label; C, emerging; D, experimental). Menopausal hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and prevents bone loss during use; the 2025–2026 FDA labelling revisions altered risk communication rather than the underlying evidence, and professional responses diverged. Fezolinetant and elinzanetant provide mechanism-based non-hormonal options, while SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), CBT for insomnia, and clinical hypnosis remain evidence-supported. Exercise, yoga, acupuncture, soy, and equol are not guideline-recommended for reducing vasomotor symptom frequency despite benefits in other domains. Gut and genitourinary microbiome findings should not be conflated: pooled evidence identifies no consistent postmenopausal gut signature, whereas vaginal Lactobacillus depletion is more reproducible but does not reliably predict symptom resolution. Evidence-based personalisation therefore remains principally clinical; microbiome sequencing, equol testing, and multi-omic treatment selection require prospective test-guided validation.

Menopause is a natural biological transition in a woman’s life, usually occurring between 45 and 55 years of age, and is defined retrospectively by 12 consecutive months of amenorrhea in the absence of another physiological or pathological cause. The preceding menopausal transition is characterized by variable ovarian function and may extend over several years. Because life expectancy substantially exceeds the average age at natural menopause for most women, many spend a considerable proportion of adult life after the final menstrual period.

By 2030, an estimated 1.2 billion women worldwide will be postmenopausal, with approximately 47 million entering the transition each year [1]. Vasomotor symptoms (VMSs), sleep disturbance, mood symptoms, genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), sexual symptoms, and musculoskeletal complaints vary substantially among individuals and populations and can impair quality of life and work participation [2,3,4,5]. Recent meta-analytic evidence reinforces that symptom burden is associated with interacting demographic, behavioral, psychosocial, and health factors rather than a single biological determinant [3].

Contemporary menopause care is increasingly shaped by a tension between established guideline-supported management and rapidly expanding claims of individualized or “precision” treatment. Major professional societies and clinical guidelines provide increasingly detailed recommendations for menopausal hormone therapy, non-hormonal pharmacotherapy, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, premature ovarian insufficiency, and the management of women with relevant comorbidities. In parallel, emerging approaches based on neurokinin signalling, microbiome composition, phytoestrogen metabolism, pharmacokinetic variation, and multi-omic profiling have been proposed as potential tools for more individualized treatment selection. However, these approaches differ substantially in evidentiary maturity, regulatory status, reproducibility, and demonstrated clinical utility. Biologically plausible mechanisms and statistically significant associations do not necessarily translate into validated treatment-selection tools or improved patient outcomes. A critical distinction is therefore needed between personalisation that can already be implemented in routine clinical practice and precision-medicine strategies that remain investigational.

The therapeutic landscape has changed through reappraisal of MHT evidence, approval of neurokinin receptor antagonists, and increasing interest in lifestyle, nutritional, microbiome, and multi-omic approaches. The central question is therefore not only which treatments are available, but which dimensions of personalisation are clinically actionable now. For clinicians, treatment selection also requires balancing multiple therapeutic options with likely long-term adherence and socioeconomic barriers. A clear synthesis of established and emerging approaches can help place these choices in context. In this review, clinical personalisation refers to treatment selection based on symptom phenotype, age and timing, uterine status, reproductive needs, contraindications, comorbidities, drug interactions, previous response, access, cost, and informed preference. Precision medicine is used more narrowly for biomarker-, microbiome-, pharmacokinetic-, or multi-omic-guided treatment selection. The objective is to evaluate established and emerging strategies within an explicit clinical-actionability framework and to identify where plausible mechanisms have, and have not, translated into validated clinical decision tools. Accordingly, the purpose of this review is not to propose an alternative set of menopause recommendations, but to critically map current guideline-supported care against emerging precision-medicine strategies and to identify where evidence remains insufficient for routine clinical implementation.

The original structured narrative search of PubMed/MEDLINE covered literature published from 1 January 2020 to 31 July 2026. Search concepts included menopause, perimenopause, MHT, VMS, neurokinin receptor antagonists, fezolinetant, elinzanetant, GSM, estrobolome, gut and vaginal microbiomes, phytoestrogens, isoflavones, equol, CBT, clinical hypnosis, lifestyle, POI, breast cancer, and surgical menopause. For the present revision, targeted update searches through 20 August 2026 were performed in PubMed/MEDLINE and official regulator or professional-society sources to identify new guidelines, systematic reviews, phase 3 trials, safety communications, and labelling changes. Current documents from the FDA, EMA, North American Menopause Society, International Menopause Society, British Menopause Society, NICE, ESHRE, ASRM, and European Society of Endocrinology were cross-checked. Key publications were selected by prioritising current clinical guidelines and regulatory documents for practice recommendations, systematic reviews/meta-analyses for evidence synthesis, and pivotal randomized trials for treatment efficacy and safety. Landmark studies published before 2020 were identified from the reference lists of major contemporary guidelines and reviews and were retained when they established widely used staging criteria, mechanisms, or pivotal clinical evidence that remained relevant to current practice. Core search domains are provided in Appendix A.

English-language guidelines, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, major prospective cohorts, and clinically relevant regulatory documents were prioritized. For therapeutic recommendations, priority was given to current clinical-practice guidelines, professional-society position statements, consensus documents, and regulatory sources; individual trials were primarily used to quantify efficacy, safety, or areas in which guideline recommendations remain incomplete. Observational, translational, in vitro, and animal studies were included when human interventional evidence was limited, but were treated as mechanistic or emerging evidence rather than as a basis for routine recommendations. Conference abstracts and company-reported results were retained only for investigational therapies lacking a full peer-reviewed publication and are explicitly identified as preliminary. When clinical evidence, guideline recommendations, and regulatory status did not align, these dimensions were reported separately: regulatory sources defined approved indications and mandatory safety requirements within a jurisdiction; guidelines informed clinical practice recommendations; and trial or observational evidence informed estimates of efficacy and risk. No single source type was assumed to override the others outside its appropriate role.

Evidence was synthesized narratively according to intervention type, symptom domain, regulatory status, study design, and clinical applicability. Because this is not a systematic review, no formal risk-of-bias instrument, meta-analysis, GRADE certainty assessment, duplicate independent screening, or exhaustive study-count denominator was used. The search should therefore not be interpreted as an exhaustive enumeration of all eligible studies, and selective inclusion remains a potential source of review-level bias. To reduce this limitation, priority was given to current guidelines, regulatory documents, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and pivotal randomized trials, with older studies retained only when they remained foundational. The review emphasizes the distinction between clinical actionability and biological plausibility. The actionability tiers below are descriptive and are not intended to replace formal guideline grading.

The actionability tier is assigned to a specific intervention (or test) for a specified indication and patient population; it should not be interpreted as a global grade for that intervention in all clinical circumstances. Tier A denotes established care supported by a current major guideline recommendation and/or regulatory approval for the stated indication, typically with randomized or long-term clinical evidence. Tier B denotes evidence-supported adjunctive or commonly off-label care with clinically meaningful human interventional evidence but less consistent regulatory or guideline status. Tier C denotes emerging human evidence that is mechanistically plausible or associative/interventional but is not validated for routine treatment selection. Tier D denotes preclinical, experimental, or currently unsupported strategies for the stated clinical use. Assignment reflected convergence of regulatory status, guideline position, study design, consistency, and clinical applicability. Where these sources diverged, the tier reflected the practical readiness of the specific use rather than a numerical evidence score, and the text or tables identify the relevant regulatory or guideline caveat. These clinical-actionability tiers describe readiness for practice; they are not substitutes for GRADE certainty ratings or formal risk-of-bias assessment. The framework is applied to the summary tables and the treatment-selection figure presented in the following sections.

path: 3. Biology and Staging of the Menopausal Transition
sections.text:
The menopausal transition is driven principally by progressive depletion and reduced competence of the ovarian follicular pool. Follicular loss accelerates with reproductive ageing and is accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction, altered DNA repair, oxidative stress, stromal and immune changes, and impaired granulosa-cell function [6,7]. These mechanisms are biologically interconnected, but their relative contribution in individual women remains incompletely defined.

Anti-Müllerian hormone. AMH is produced by granulosa cells of preantral and small antral follicles and is a useful marker of ovarian reserve. Concentrations decline with reproductive ageing, but AMH should not be used alone to diagnose perimenopause or menopause in otherwise healthy women of typical menopausal age. Ovarian reserve reflects follicle quantity rather than oocyte quality, and AMH does not capture the fluctuating endocrine changes that characterize the menopausal transition. Its value is greater in fertility assessment, research, and selected situations involving suspected premature ovarian insufficiency or iatrogenic ovarian damage [7].

STRAW+10 staging. The STRAW+10 criteria provide a widely used framework for reproductive ageing based primarily on menstrual-cycle characteristics, with supportive endocrine and ovarian-reserve markers where appropriate (Table 1) [8]. Fixed hormone thresholds should be interpreted cautiously because concentrations fluctuate substantially during the transition. Consistent with the 2025 European Society of Endocrinology guideline, routine biochemical testing is not necessary to diagnose or manage typical perimenopause or menopause in women older than 45 years; testing is more relevant in younger women when early menopause or POI is suspected [9].

The KNDy neuronal circuit and vasomotor symptoms. KNDy neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus co-express kisspeptin (KISS1), neurokinin B (NKB), and dynorphin A (PDYN), functioning as the central GnRH pulse generator. With estrogen withdrawal, KNDy neurons hypertrophy histologically, increase NKB and kisspeptin expression markedly, and hyperactivate NK3R-mediated neurotransmission, projecting to the median preoptic nucleus (MnPO) where NK3R activation triggers heat dissipation effectors: cutaneous vasodilation, sweating, and the subjective hot flash (Figure 1). This model provides the mechanistic rationale for NK3R antagonism and directly enabled development of the agents discussed in Section 5. It should nevertheless be described as the leading model rather than a complete account, because the relative contribution of NK1R-mediated signalling and of non-hypothalamic pathways to individual symptom burden remains under investigation [10,11].

Estrogen receptors and systemic consequences. ERα, ERβ, and GPER have overlapping but distinct tissue distributions and signaling effects. Estrogen decline contributes to accelerated bone loss, changes in body composition, adverse lipid and vascular changes, and progressive vulvovaginal and urinary symptoms [6]. Associations with cognition, neurodegeneration, sarcopenia, and cardiovascular disease are biologically plausible and epidemiologically important, but causal pathways and treatment effects differ by age, timing, formulation, and baseline health.

Ethnic and individual variability. The SWAN cohort and a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrate variation in VMS presence, severity, and duration across population groups [3,12]. These differences are associated with interacting biological, psychosocial, socioeconomic, behavioral, environmental, and health-care factors. Smoking, obesity, depression, education, and income are among the factors associated with symptom patterns in pooled observational evidence [3]. Dietary patterns and microbial metabolism may contribute, but current evidence does not support attributing population differences primarily to genetics, equol-producing status, or microbiome composition.

MHT remains the most effective treatment for moderate-to-severe VMS and is effective for prevention of bone loss while treatment continues; low-dose vaginal estrogen is highly effective for GSM. For most healthy symptomatic women younger than 60 years or within 10 years of the final menstrual period, the benefit–risk profile is generally favourable after assessment of contraindications and individual risk factors [9,13,14,15,16]. Recent regulatory activity has changed the framing of MHT without changing the underlying evidence base, and this distinction requires explicit statement before the clinical evidence is reviewed.

The 2025–2026 labelling change. In November 2025, the FDA requested class-wide labelling revisions for menopausal hormone therapy and, on 12 February 2026, approved revised labels for the first six products across systemic and local categories. Risk statements on cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and probable dementia were removed from the boxed warnings, while relevant cardiovascular and breast-cancer information remains elsewhere in systemic labels and the endometrial-cancer boxed warning remains for systemic estrogen-alone therapy in women with a uterus [17,18,19]. This was a change in risk communication rather than new randomised evidence; product-specific benefit–risk assessment by formulation, route, age, timing, comorbidity, and indication remains essential.

International interpretation. Regulatory and professional responses have not been identical. The Menopause Society supported removal of the boxed warning from low-dose vaginal estrogen while emphasizing individualized risk discussion for systemic therapy [20]. EMAS welcomed the FDA decision but explicitly cautioned that removal of a warning does not make MHT universally indicated [21]. The International Menopause Society supported removal for vaginal estrogen and scientific review of systemic warnings, but did not support removing all systemic warnings [22]. European clinicians should continue to follow EMA/MHRA and national product information. Across jurisdictions, MHT remains indicated principally for symptom treatment and, in selected women, prevention of bone loss rather than primary prevention of cardiovascular disease or dementia [9,13,14,15,16,23,24].

Timing and treatment goals. Age and time since menopause influence the absolute risks associated with systemic MHT. Initiation in younger, recently menopausal women generally has a more favorable benefit–risk profile than initiation in older women or more than 10 years after menopause. The ELITE trial showed a slower increase in carotid intima–media thickness when oral estradiol was initiated within 6 years of menopause, but not when initiated 10 or more years after menopause; this surrogate outcome does not establish MHT as a treatment for prevention of cardiovascular events [25]. Large register-based analyses of contemporary MHT show that cardiovascular risk varies by formulation and route; because these data are observational, they remain susceptible to confounding and do not establish a preventive indication [26]. MHT should be prescribed primarily for symptom treatment and, in selected women, prevention of bone loss rather than for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease or dementia.

Route of administration and thrombotic risk. Oral estrogen undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism and is associated with a higher venous thromboembolism risk than non-use. Observational evidence suggests that standard-dose transdermal estradiol may have a lower thrombotic risk than oral estrogen, although direct randomized comparisons for clinical events are limited [27]. Transdermal estradiol is therefore often preferred for women with obesity, migraine, hypertriglyceridemia, gallbladder disease, or elevated baseline thrombotic risk, but route selection should remain individualized. Where systemic MHT is indicated, the formulation and route should be selected according to individual clinical factors and current product information. Transdermal 17β-estradiol avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism, but absorbed exposure can vary between preparations and individuals; this does not justify a universal preference for a single route in all patients [9,13,14,15,16,27].

Progestogen and endometrial protection. Women with an intact uterus receiving systemic estrogen require adequate progestogen or another evidence-based endometrial-protection strategy. Observational studies suggest that micronised progesterone and dydrogesterone may have a more favourable breast-safety profile than some synthetic progestogens, but comparative randomised evidence is limited and risk is influenced by duration and regimen [28,29]. A levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system can provide contraception and endometrial protection when combined with systemic estrogen, although licensing and recommended duration vary by jurisdiction. The requirement for progestogen is determined primarily by uterine and endometrial status. After total hysterectomy, estrogen-only systemic MHT is generally appropriate because endometrial protection is no longer required, although exceptions may apply in specific clinical contexts [9,13,14,15,16].

Perimenopause-specific considerations. MHT is not contraceptive. In women who still require contraception, options include combined hormonal contraception for medically eligible women or a progestogen method, particularly a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, combined with systemic estrogen when required for symptoms. Regimen choice should account for bleeding pattern, migraine, smoking, blood pressure, thrombotic risk, and reproductive plans.

Unscheduled bleeding and follow-up. Bleeding is common during the first months of continuous combined MHT and may also occur with sequential regimens. Persistent, heavy, new-onset, or recurrent bleeding after an established amenorrhoeic interval requires assessment according to age, regimen, endometrial risk factors, and local guidance. Dose, adherence, drug interactions, and adequacy of progestogen exposure should be reviewed before or alongside investigation. The 2025 European Society of Endocrinology guideline recommends reassessing symptom response and tolerability approximately 3 months after MHT initiation, with dose or formulation adjustment when response is inadequate or adverse effects occur, followed by periodic reassessment thereafter [9]. NICE guidance was further updated in April 2026 regarding unscheduled bleeding during systemic MHT [30]. Table 2 summarises the contemporary evidence for major clinical outcomes and highlights where formulation, route, and study design affect interpretation.

path: Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: Treatment Selection and Special Considerations
sections.text:
GSM includes vulvovaginal dryness, burning or irritation, dyspareunia and other sexual symptoms, and urinary symptoms such as urgency, dysuria, and recurrent urinary tract infection. Treatment should be matched to the predominant symptom and severity rather than assuming that all genitourinary complaints have the same mechanism. Non-hormonal vaginal moisturisers are used regularly to improve baseline dryness, whereas lubricants are used primarily to reduce friction and pain during sexual activity; either can be used alone or together with local hormonal treatment [30]. Pelvic-floor assessment and therapy are appropriate when pelvic-floor overactivity, pain, urinary dysfunction, or musculoskeletal contributors coexist, and persistent dyspareunia warrants evaluation for dermatological, infectious, pelvic-floor, and other vulvovaginal causes.

For women without a history of breast cancer, low-dose vaginal estrogen has the most robust evidence for persistent GSM and can be delivered as cream, gel, tablet/pessary, or a vaginal ring according to preference, availability, and local labelling [30,31]. Systemic MHT is not required when GSM is the only indication. Vaginal prasterone (DHEA) is an option when vaginal estrogen or non-hormonal measures are ineffective or not tolerated, while oral ospemifene can be considered when local treatment is impractical or unsuitable [30]. Vaginal estrogen may also reduce recurrent urinary-tract infections in peri- and postmenopausal women and should be considered within the broader recurrent-UTI pathway rather than as systemic prophylaxis [30].

Energy-based vaginal laser and radiofrequency therapies should not be presented as established alternatives to approved GSM treatments. The 2025 AUA/SUFU/AUGS guideline concluded that current evidence does not support routine CO2 laser, Er:YAG laser, or radiofrequency treatment for GSM outcomes; if considered outside a trial for a woman who cannot use or declines established options, the experimental status and uncertainty regarding long-term efficacy and safety should be explicit [31].

For women who have a contraindication to systemic MHT, prefer not to use hormones, or have an inadequate response, several non-hormonal options are available. Neurokinin receptor antagonists target thermoregulatory signaling downstream of estrogen withdrawal without estrogenic or progestogenic activity. Other options, including selected SSRIs or SNRIs, gabapentin, and oxybutynin, act through different pathways and have distinct adverse-effect and interaction profiles.

Fezolinetant (45 mg once daily). Fezolinetant was approved by the FDA in May 2023 and received European Union marketing authorization in December 2023 [32]. In SKYLIGHT 1 and 2, placebo-adjusted reductions in moderate-to-severe VMS frequency were approximately 2 to 3 episodes per day at weeks 4 and 12 [33,34], with associated improvement in menopause-related quality of life in pooled analysis [35]. Post-marketing reports of serious liver injury led the FDA to add a boxed warning in December 2024. Baseline hepatic tests and follow-up testing monthly for the first 3 months and at months 6 and 9 are required in the United States [36]. Access differs by jurisdiction: in the United Kingdom, NICE technology appraisal guidance issued in 2026 recommends fezolinetant as an option for moderate-to-severe VMS when MHT is unsuitable [37].

Elinzanetant (120 mg once daily at bedtime). Elinzanetant was approved by the FDA in October 2025 as a dual NK1 and NK3 receptor antagonist. In OASIS 1 and 2, placebo-adjusted mean reductions in VMS frequency at week 12 were approximately 3.2 episodes per day, with improvements in sleep disturbance and menopause-related quality of life [38]. OASIS 3 reported a smaller placebo-adjusted effect in a broader population and provided 52-week safety data [39]. The US label requires baseline hepatic testing and repeat transaminase assessment at 3 months; moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment is not recommended [40]. In OASIS 4, women with VMS related to endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer or risk reduction had a week-12 least-squares mean difference of −3.4 moderate-to-severe VMS episodes per day versus placebo (95% CI −4.2 to −2.5) [41]. No head-to-head trial has compared elinzanetant with fezolinetant. Differences between numerical effect estimates from separate trials must not be interpreted as evidence that one agent is more effective, because trial populations, baseline symptom burden, protocols, estimands, and placebo responses differ. OASIS 4 provides evidence for VMS efficacy in an oncology population but does not establish long-term oncological safety or breast-cancer recurrence outcomes. Table 3 compares the two approved neurokinin-targeted therapies using similar outcome metrics and current regulatory monitoring requirements.

Cendifensine (NOE-115) is an investigational monoamine reuptake modulator in phase 2 development. Preliminary phase 2a results reported substantial reductions from baseline in VMS frequency and possible effects on mood, appetite, and fatigue, but these findings have not yet been confirmed in a large peer-reviewed randomised phase 3 trial. The agent is therefore discussed only as an emerging therapy [42].

SSRIs and SNRIs. Paroxetine, venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, escitalopram, and citalopram are antidepressant drugs that have evidence for reducing VMS, although effect sizes are generally smaller than with systemic MHT [43]. Low-dose paroxetine is FDA-approved for VMS; other agents are frequently used off-label. Paroxetine and fluoxetine strongly inhibit CYP2D6 and are generally avoided with tamoxifen because they can reduce formation of its active metabolite, whereas venlafaxine and citalopram or escitalopram have less CYP2D6 inhibition.

Gabapentin, oxybutynin, and testosterone. Gabapentin is an anticonvulsant that can reduce VMS and may be useful when nocturnal symptoms or sleep disturbance predominate, although dizziness and somnolence can limit use. Oxybutynin (an anticholinergic drug primarily used for overactive bladder) can reduce VMS in randomized placebo-controlled trials, including in women with breast cancer, but its anticholinergic adverse-effect profile warrants caution in older women or those with cognitive risk [44]. GSM treatment is discussed separately in Section Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: Treatment Selection and Special Considerations. Systemic transdermal testosterone has evidence for postmenopausal hypoactive sexual desire disorder after biopsychosocial assessment, but it is not a general treatment for fatigue, cognition, or wellbeing and is off-label in many countries [45].

Medication review and interactions. Interaction risk is a recurring determinant of treatment selection across hormonal and non-hormonal care. Table 4 summarizes selected high-impact interactions that are most likely to change prescribing decisions; it is deliberately not exhaustive and should be interpreted alongside current product information.

path: 6. Microbiome, Phytoestrogens, and the Boundary of Precision Medicine
sections.text: The estrobolome describes the aggregate microbial genes and enzymes capable of metabolising estrogens, particularly through deconjugation of biliary estrogen metabolites [46,47,48]. The biochemical mechanism is plausible and experimentally demonstrable, but the clinically relevant magnitude of microbiome-mediated estrogen recycling in humans remains uncertain. This section therefore uses the microbiome and phytoestrogen literature as a test case for the boundary between mechanism-based personalization and validated precision medicine: evidence is separated into mechanistic, observational, interventional, and treatment-selection levels (Figure 2).

path: 6. Microbiome, Phytoestrogens, and the Boundary of Precision Medicine
sections.text:
Biochemical foundations. Estrogens produced by the ovaries and peripheral tissues undergo hepatic metabolism and conjugation before biliary or urinary excretion. In the intestine, microbial β-glucuronidases and other enzymes can deconjugate selected metabolites, permitting reabsorption [47,48]. This mechanism is established biochemically, but its quantitative importance varies by substrate, enzyme class, microbial community, intestinal transit, medication exposure, and host metabolism.

Experimental evidence demonstrates that specific microbial β-glucuronidases can reactivate estrogen glucuronides [47]. Reviews have identified additional microbial enzymes potentially involved in estrogen metabolism [48]. These observations support the concept of a microbiome–endocrine interface, but they do not by themselves demonstrate that changing microbiome composition improves clinical menopause outcomes.

Microbiome changes across menopause. Cross-sectional studies have reported differences in microbial composition between premenopausal and postmenopausal groups, but findings vary by age, adiposity, diet, medication use, geography, sequencing method, and analytic pipeline [52]. Importantly, a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of seven studies found no significant difference in gut alpha-diversity, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, or the Bacteroidetes-to-Firmicutes ratio between hypoestrogenic and euestrogenic groups, with substantial heterogeneity across studies [49]. No universal postmenopausal gut microbiome signature has therefore been established, and individual taxa or diversity scores should not be interpreted as diagnostic or treatment-selection biomarkers.

Proposed systemic consequences and unresolved mechanisms. Reduced short-chain-fatty-acid production and impaired intestinal-barrier function are plausible links between dysbiosis, inflammation, and cardiometabolic risk, but human studies mainly demonstrate associations rather than causality. Estrogen exposure can in turn influence microbial ecology, while microbial metabolism can affect the pool of deconjugated estrogen metabolites; evidence for a self-reinforcing clinical feedback loop between MHT, microbial beta-glucuronidase activity, and systemic estrogen concentrations remains preliminary and is better presented as a testable model than as a confirmed therapeutic mechanism. Common medicines can also alter gut microbial composition, and microbial enzymes can modify the disposition of some drugs and endogenous compounds, but in menopause care this remains an emerging research question rather than an established explanation for interindividual variation in MHT response. Large, well-controlled longitudinal cohorts, prospective pharmacokinetic studies, and intervention trials are needed to determine whether microbiome changes contribute independently to menopause symptoms or primarily reflect ageing and related exposures, and are required before microbiome profiles could guide prescribing.

Microbiome-directed interventions. A small randomised trial reported that a probiotic formulation with beta-glucuronidase activity altered serum estrogen measures in peri- and postmenopausal women [53]. However, proof of a biochemical effect is not proof of symptom benefit or of a clinically useful treatment-selection strategy. A 2026 systematic review of Lactobacillus-based interventions for GSM identified only nine studies with 751 participants and found limited, heterogeneous evidence for lower urinary-tract and vaginal outcomes [51]. Current evidence does not establish a strain, dose, duration, target phenotype, or routine menopause indication for probiotic prescribing. Dietary fibre supports microbial diversity and short-chain-fatty-acid production and should be encouraged for general cardiometabolic and gastrointestinal health, but claims that specific prebiotics reliably restore an estrogen-supportive microbiome remain unproven. Faecal microbiota transplantation is not an established treatment for menopause symptoms and should remain confined to approved indications or research protocols.

path: 6. Microbiome, Phytoestrogens, and the Boundary of Precision Medicine
sections.text:
Evidence is more consistent for the genitourinary than for the gut microbiome. Declining estrogen reduces epithelial glycogen and is commonly associated with higher vaginal pH, reduced Lactobacillus dominance, and greater microbial diversity. A 2026 systematic review of 23 studies involving 5027 participants found consistent postmenopausal Lactobacillus depletion and greater microbial diversity across genitourinary studies, although associations between specific community states and individual GSM symptoms were weaker and heterogeneous [50].

Low-dose vaginal estrogen improves GSM and can partially restore a more Lactobacillus-dominant environment, but microbiome restoration does not uniformly predict clinical symptom resolution [50]. Vaginal probiotics have variable and limited evidence and should not substitute for established GSM therapy [51]. Next-generation sequencing remains valuable in research but is not routinely recommended for diagnosis or treatment selection in postmenopausal women [50,54]. Gut and vaginal microbiome findings should therefore not be conflated: the direction and clinical meaning of diversity differ by anatomical site.

path: 6. Microbiome, Phytoestrogens, and the Boundary of Precision Medicine
sections.text:
Chemistry and receptor activity. Isoflavones, lignans, and coumestans are plant-derived compounds that can interact with estrogen receptors and other signalling pathways. Genistein generally has greater affinity for ERβ than ERα, but receptor-binding observations do not translate directly into tissue-selective clinical safety or efficacy. Preparation, dose, metabolism, and baseline diet contribute to heterogeneous trial results [55,56,57]. Isoflavones include genistein, daidzein, and glycitein from soy and related compounds from red clover. Lignans from flaxseed and sesame are converted by gut bacteria to enterolignans. Daidzein can be converted to S-equol by specific microbial communities, creating a measurable metabolic phenotype that may influence exposure to active metabolites.

Equol-producing status. Approximately 30–50% of adults in many Western cohorts and a higher proportion in some Asian cohorts produce measurable equol after soy or daidzein exposure [55]. Producer status is better described as a pharmacomicrobiomic or microbiome-dependent metabolic phenotype than as a pharmacogenomic variable. Some studies suggest differential responses to isoflavones, but results are inconsistent and do not yet validate equol testing as a routine treatment-selection tool. Urinary equol measurement after a standardised soy or daidzein challenge and metagenomic detection of equol-producing pathways are research tools. Non-producers may still respond to genistein or other isoflavones through equol-independent mechanisms. Preformed S-equol products are available in some markets, but comparative effectiveness and long-term safety data remain insufficient to support a universal phenotype-guided algorithm.

Clinical evidence. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials found a small improvement in overall menopausal symptom scores with soy isoflavones, but no significant treatment effect on hot flushes, excessive sweating, insomnia, or the vasomotor-symptom domain [56]. A separate 2024 meta-analysis of five RCTs involving 425 women found no significant improvement in overall menopausal symptoms or quality of life, although depression scores improved [58]. These findings support, at most, modest and domain-specific effects rather than use of soy isoflavones as an evidence-based substitute for MHT or approved neurokinin antagonists for VMS. Preparation, dose, adherence, background diet, and metabolic phenotype remain important sources of heterogeneity. Trials have also examined bone density, lipids, glucose metabolism, vascular function, mood, and cognition, but findings are inconsistent and generally insufficient to establish phytoestrogen supplements as alternatives to osteoporosis, cardiovascular, or neurocognitive therapies; mechanistic and preclinical findings should be separated from clinical outcomes. The main phytoestrogen classes, their mechanisms, human evidence, and limitations are summarised in Table 5.

Safety and product quality. Dietary soy foods are generally considered safe for most women, including many breast-cancer survivors, whereas concentrated supplements require greater caution because dose, purity, labelling, and interactions vary. EFSA previously found no signal of harm to breast, thyroid, or uterine tissue at commonly studied supplemental doses in postmenopausal women [57]. Reassuringly, a 2025 meta-analysis of 40 randomized trials (3285 participants) found no statistically significant effect of soy isoflavones on endometrial thickness, vaginal maturation index, FSH, or circulating estradiol [59]. These data address selected measures of estrogenicity but do not eliminate the need for product-quality assessment or oncology-specific clinical judgement.

Mediterranean-style dietary pattern. A dietary pattern rich in vegetables, legumes, whole grains, nuts, olive oil, fish, and minimally processed foods supports cardiovascular, metabolic, and bone health. It also supplies fibre and polyphenols that influence microbial ecology. Evidence for direct reduction of VMS is less consistent than evidence for broader health benefits; dietary counselling should therefore emphasise overall health, adequate protein and calcium, and sustainable weight management rather than promising symptom-specific effects [60].

Behavioural and lifestyle interventions are important components of comprehensive menopause care, but their effects must be reported by outcome rather than treated as a single category. An intervention can improve symptom bother, sleep, mood, physical function, bone health, or cardiometabolic risk without materially reducing physiological VMS frequency. This distinction is central to avoiding overstatement and is summarised in Table 6 [43,61].

Cognitive behavioural therapy, including CBT for insomnia. Menopause-specific CBT reduces VMS-related bother, interference, anxiety, and sleep disturbance even when objective hot-flash frequency changes little [30,62]. CBT is therefore complementary to pharmacological treatment rather than a direct substitute for the thermoregulatory effects of MHT or neurokinin antagonists. CBT-I has specific evidence for menopausal insomnia rather than for direct suppression of VMS. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 RCTs involving 973 women found improvements in sleep quality and insomnia severity across face-to-face, telephone, and internet-delivered formats [63]. CBT-I should therefore be considered a targeted treatment for insomnia in peri- and postmenopausal women, while nocturnal VMS and other contributors are managed in parallel.

Clinical hypnosis. A 2025 scoping review identified 23 studies and concluded that clinical-hypnosis studies reported reductions in hot-flash frequency and severity, whereas CBT studies more consistently improved bother and interference [64]. The evidence base remains smaller than that for established pharmacological treatments, and comparisons across interventions are indirect. A pivotal randomised trial reported a 74% reduction in hot-flash scores with clinical hypnosis compared with 17% with structured attention control [65]. These findings are promising, but they should not be interpreted as demonstrating equivalence to fezolinetant or elinzanetant because populations, outcomes, placebo controls, and trial designs differ. Access to trained practitioners and the need for repeated sessions remain practical limitations.

Mindfulness, yoga, and relaxation. These interventions may be useful for stress, mood, physical function, flexibility, or subjective wellbeing in selected women, but this should be separated from claims of VMS treatment. The 2023 North American Menopause Society position statement did not recommend exercise, yoga, mindfulness-based interventions, relaxation, cooling techniques, trigger avoidance, soy/equol, or acupuncture as evidence-based treatments for reducing VMS because results were negative, inconsistent, or insufficient [43]. They can still be offered for other appropriate health goals when expectations are explicit and patient preference supports their use.

Physical activity and structured exercise. Regular aerobic activity and resistance training should be actively encouraged for cardiometabolic health, maintenance of muscle and physical function, psychological wellbeing, and bone-health support. These benefits are clinically important in midlife and after menopause, but exercise should not be presented as an established treatment for reducing hot-flash frequency; the 2023 North American Menopause Society statement did not recommend it for that specific indication [43,61]. Resistance training deserves particular emphasis because preservation of lean mass and strength is a meaningful menopause-health goal independent of VMS response.

Weight management and anti-obesity pharmacotherapy. Weight reduction in women with overweight or obesity may reduce VMS and improve cardiometabolic risk, sleep apnoea, mobility, and several cancer-related risk factors. GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists should be prescribed according to established obesity or diabetes indications rather than as menopause treatments. A 2026 retrospective cohort found greater tirzepatide-associated weight loss among MHT users than non-users, but residual confounding prevents causal interpretation and randomised studies are required [66].

Sleep disturbance and behavioral sleep treatment. Sleep problems during the menopausal transition are heterogeneous and may reflect VMS-related awakenings, insomnia, depression or anxiety, obstructive sleep apnoea, restless legs, medicines, alcohol, pain, or other contributors. Management should therefore identify the dominant mechanism rather than assuming that all sleep disturbance is caused directly by estrogen withdrawal. CBT-I has the strongest targeted behavioural evidence for menopausal insomnia [63]. MHT can improve sleep when nocturnal VMS are a major driver, and elinzanetant improved sleep outcomes in VMS trials, but it should not be described as a treatment for primary insomnia in the absence of VMS. Screening and treatment for sleep apnoea, mood disorders, and other sleep disorders remain important.

Acupuncture. Acupuncture studies for menopausal VMS are difficult to interpret because sham controls can have substantial contextual and physiological effects, and real acupuncture has not consistently outperformed sham treatment for hot-flash frequency. Pragmatic comparisons with waiting-list or no-treatment controls may show patient-reported improvement, but these designs do not establish a specific VMS effect. The 2023 North American Menopause Society position statement therefore classified acupuncture as not recommended for VMS treatment on the available evidence [43]. It may still be chosen for other indications or as a patient-preferred complementary intervention when expectations, cost, and evidence uncertainty are discussed.

Dietary and environmental strategies. Alcohol, caffeine, spicy foods, heat, and other exposures are reported as triggers by some women, but controlled evidence does not support universal avoidance as a treatment for VMS [43]. Individual symptom diaries can be useful when a reproducible trigger is suspected, and cooling or layered clothing may improve comfort without being described as disease-modifying therapy. Calcium and vitamin D intake should be assessed according to diet, fracture risk, and local osteoporosis guidance; routine high-dose supplementation for all postmenopausal women is not supported.

Menopause management should not be approached as a uniform clinical entity. Premature ovarian insufficiency, treatment-induced menopause, breast-cancer endocrine therapy, surgical menopause, and major differences in access to care require modified risk–benefit assessment and coordinated management.

Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), defined by loss of ovarian activity before age 40, occurs in at least 1–3% of women in contemporary guidance and differs fundamentally from natural menopause because of the longer duration of estrogen deficiency and its implications for bone, cardiovascular, sexual, reproductive, and psychological health [9,67]. Causes include genetic, autoimmune, iatrogenic, and idiopathic forms. Diagnosis and treatment should follow current POI-specific guidance rather than routine natural-menopause pathways.

In the absence of a contraindication, physiological-dose hormone replacement is generally recommended until approximately the usual age of natural menopause [67]. Regimens and doses should be individualised, and adequate endometrial protection is required for women with a uterus. Fertility counselling, bone-density assessment, cardiovascular risk management, psychological support, and evaluation for associated genetic or autoimmune conditions may be required. AMH can contribute to assessment after gonadotoxic treatment but should not be used as the sole determinant of long-term outcomes [68].

Systemic MHT is generally not recommended in women with a previous breast cancer diagnosis, particularly after hormone-receptor-positive disease [57]. Exceptional cases with severe refractory symptoms may require multidisciplinary shared decision-making after non-hormonal options have failed. OASIS 4 provides important contemporary evidence: among women with moderate-to-severe VMS related to endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer or risk reduction, elinzanetant produced a week-12 placebo-adjusted least-squares mean difference of −3.4 episodes per day (95% CI −4.2 to −2.5) [41]; this efficacy result should not be interpreted as evidence of long-term oncological safety. Venlafaxine, citalopram, escitalopram, gabapentin, CBT, and clinical hypnosis may also be considered according to symptom phenotype and drug interactions. For GSM, moisturisers and lubricants are first-line. When symptoms remain clinically important, low-dose vaginal estrogen can be considered after individual risk–benefit discussion, but endocrine therapy matters: use alongside tamoxifen is generally considered less concerning mechanistically because tamoxifen blocks the estrogen receptor in breast tissue, whereas women receiving aromatase inhibitors require more cautious multidisciplinary shared decision-making because exogenous estrogen is not receptor-blocked and transient systemic absorption may be relevant [9,30,69]. Vaginal DHEA or other prescription options may be considered when vaginal estrogen is unsuitable, but local labelling, oncology guidance, and the limited long-term safety evidence should be reviewed [69].

Surgical menopause following bilateral oophorectomy differs fundamentally from natural menopause because ovarian hormone production ceases abruptly rather than declining progressively over several years. When bilateral oophorectomy is performed before the usual age of natural menopause, women may experience more severe vasomotor symptoms, sleep disturbance, mood changes, sexual dysfunction, and genitourinary symptoms.
